speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to draw the attention of the House to a report which was published in the Montreal ' Gazette ' on Monday as a special from Ottawa, It reads as follows:
Ottawa, July 23 (special).-The revolt of the supporters of the government from the province of Quebec against the calling of the extra session in midsummer for the sole purpose of carrying on a hopeless attempt to put through the reciprocity agreement, does not show any signs of dying down.

maintopic: NEWSPAPER STATEMENT WITH REGARD TO QUEBEC MEMBERS.

maintopic: NEWSPAPER STATEMENT WITH REGARD TO QUEBEC MEMBERS.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: NEWSPAPER STATEMENT WITH REGARD TO QUEBEC MEMBERS.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: NEWSPAPER STATEMENT WITH REGARD TO QUEBEC MEMBERS.
speechtext:
Yes.
Mr. SMYTH (Algomai
Up to Friday a large number of French Canadian Liberal members had ignored the urgent call of the whips and failed to put in an appearance at Ottawa,

maintopic: NEWSPAPER STATEMENT WITH REGARD TO QUEBEC MEMBERS.

It is well known that Sir Wilfrid Laurier was nettled at the result of the division on Tuesday-

maintopic: NEWSPAPER STATEMENT WITH REGARD TO QUEBEC MEMBERS.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: NEWSPAPER STATEMENT WITH REGARD TO QUEBEC MEMBERS.

We must consider that the applause coming from the other side is an indication that this article meets with the approval of these hon. gentlemen.

With the opposition determined to bring up from day to day matters of public importance on the motion either to go into Committee of Ways and Means or Supply, and follow these up with motions of censure and want of confidence, a strenuous effort is being made to whip the Quebec men into line.

maintopic: NEWSPAPER STATEMENT WITH REGARD TO QUEBEC MEMBERS.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: NEWSPAPER STATEMENT WITH REGARD TO QUEBEC MEMBERS.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speechtext:
I am very glad to hear this applause. We will make good use of it in time.
There is demoralization in its ranks; Lau-rier's control of his solid Quebec majority is vanishing;-

maintopic: NEWSPAPER STATEMENT WITH REGARD TO QUEBEC MEMBERS.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: NEWSPAPER STATEMENT WITH REGARD TO QUEBEC MEMBERS.
speechtext: -discipline is lacking, and those who are in attendance are chafing under the action in bringing them back when they could be much better employed, according to their way of thinking, in canvassing their constituents in view of the imminent elections.

maintopic: NEWSPAPER STATEMENT WITH REGARD TO QUEBEC MEMBERS.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: NEWSPAPER STATEMENT WITH REGARD TO QUEBEC MEMBERS.
speechtext:
The Montreal ' Gazette ' is a paper for which I have had, for a great number of years, a great deal of respect and admiration. It is quite evident that of late bad company has corrupted its good manners. I must now say to you, Mr. Speaker, that my comment shall be very short because this article is contemptible, malicious and untrue in every particular. I do r.ot know who is the author of this dispatch, but I hope that it is not the reporter of the press appointed to sit in this gallery and to occupy a place m the company of gentlemen.
It is quite true that French Canadian members of this House coming from the province of Quebec are not over burdened with wealth but there is one thing that I can say and which will appeal to the fair minded men on the other side of the House, and I hope they are many, that it is not money which brings us here in this House. We are under a strong feeling that we are discharging our duty before the country and I have to say that if the reporter of the 'Gazette', appointed in the gallery is the author of this article he deserves the censure of this House.

maintopic: NEWSPAPER STATEMENT WITH REGARD TO QUEBEC MEMBERS.
speechtext:
-(Translation.)-Mr. Speaker, the article of which the hon. member for Bellechasse complains is not an isolated one, but forms part of a plan of campaign. As a matter of fact, to-day's Montreal ' Gazette ' contains the same unpleasant insinuations. Quebec Liberals are accustomed to the calumnies of the Tory press, and this new exhibition does not disturb us; it will, however, serve to show the electors of the province what measure of justice they may expect from such opponents.
An analysis of the vote of the 18th July, Mr. Speaker, will show that at least as many French Canadian Liberals were in their seats on the first day following recess as members from other provinces, Liberal or Conservative.
There are in this House 220 members exclusive of the Speaker. The vote taken on that day gave the following result: 61 Liberals and 45 Conservatives. Only 106 members voted therefore, less than half of the whole House. The opposition mustered 45 votes out of a total of 88 members.
Allow me to call your attention to the fact that out of the Conservative contingent from the province- of Quebec two members only were present on that day, the member for Argenteuil (Mr. Perley), who is the party whip, and the hon. member for St. Ann's (Mr. Doherty); the ten other French Canadian representatives of His Majesty's opposition in the province of Quebec were all absent. The hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) was not there, nor was the hon. member for Drummond and Artha-baska (Mr. Gilbert), the champion of the new doctrine in the province of Quebec.
But the narrow fanaticism of the ' Gazette's ' views are more especially apparent in the vile insinuation that French Canadian Liberal members from Quebec weTe not here because they had no more indemnity to draw. I defy the ' Gazette ' and all the Tory press of the country to point out one single French Canadian Liberal member who ever publicly or privately made such a dishonest declaration. Such calumnies will not help to maintain among the voters of the province of Quebec that reputation.

for fairness and moderation which the ' Gazette ' had acquired. In any case there must be no misunderstanding on this point. The Liberal members from the province of Quebec are here, and here they will remain until the end of this important parliamentary struggle, and when the fight is transferred to another field, they will be found in the forefront of battle.

speechtext: Has any order in council been passed suspending the immigration regulations between ourselves and the United States so as to permit agricultural labourers to come into this country without being handicapped or bothered with _ the usual immigration questions und interrogations during the harvest so as to permit American labourers to enter Canada to assist in reaping the harvest.

speakerposition: topic
maintopic: ELECTIONS IN NORTHERN ONTARIO.
ELECTIONS IN NORTHERN ONTARIO.
speechtext:
I wish to call the attention of the ministry to an article appearing in the Montreal * Star ' entitled:
To-morrow's caucuses expected to determine question of election.
The last clause of this article reads:
While till to-morrow nothing will be conclusively known, the present outlook is for a speedy termination of parliament and polling at the end of August or beginning of September. In that event it is quite probable that elections in the Ontario constituencies with unorganized districts would be deferred. The seats are now all held by Conservatives. Under the statute, the lists for these districts are to be revised annually, between August 1st and October 15, unless otherwise ordered by special proclamation. The latter appears in Saturday's 'Canada Gazette' and it fixes the time for revision between July 18 and September. 18. This is significant of what is coming.
I would ask whether there is any truth in this article, whether it is the intention of the government, in the event of an election coming on immediately, to defer the elections in the northern part of Ontario. There is absolutely no need for doing so, the people of northern Ontario should have exactly the same rights as any other citizens of Canada. They have already been put to the trouble of having special lists prepared where the ordinary lists are quite sufficient. I spoke to the enumerators in my own district after the last revision, and I found that in seven polling subdivisions there were only two changes, and these two were of men moving from one polling subdivision to another. It is also true that large numbers were added in bush polls. The Ontario lists are prepared on a far better system than the enumeration made by this government. There is absolutely no reason, legal or otherwise for deferring the elections in northern Ontario. The people of northern Ontario are willing to have an election, we are prepared to go to the country on the issue now before parliament, but we desire to have an absolutely fair chance.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ELECTIONS IN NORTHERN ONTARIO.
speechtext: There is absolutely no occasion for such a question. My hon. friend knows that the election when it takes place, in northern Ontario, and everywhere else, will take place according to law.

maintopic: ELECTIONS IN NORTHERN ONTARIO.
speechtext:
The answer of the Prime Minister appears to me to be entirely non-committal, it does not convey anything. The right hon. gentleman was asked if the elections would be

held in the ridings in northern Ontario before the lists were prepared. His answer was that the elections would be held according to law. What we want to know is: Will the elections in those ridings be held before the lists are prepared, or will the elections be deferred-yes or no? If the elections are going to be deferred, the Prime Minister can take refuge in the quibble that that is according to the law; but if it is according to law it is not according to justice, and I think, in justice to the House, and the country he should state distinctly whether the elections in those Tidings are going to be held at the same time as the other elections, or are they going to be deferred?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ELECTIONS IN NORTHERN ONTARIO.
speechtext: My hon. friend knows that under the statutes elections can be deferred in certain constituencies and not in others. The constituencies of northern Ontario are not among those in which the elections can be deferred.

maintopic: ELECTIONS IN NORTHERN ONTARIO.
speechtext:
I wish to call the Prime Minister's attention to important changes which have taken place in east and west Hamilton since the last election. I called the attention of the Secretary of State to this months ago, because it seemed to me that it was necessary that some legislation should be passed to remedy what may be an evil. Since the last election there has been taken from the county of Wentworth and added to Hamilton West a considerable district, and a considerable population. In East Hamilton there have been other changes of perhaps much greater extent. There has been taken from the county and added to the city what was perhaps equal to 50 per cent of the old riding of Hamilton East. The description of Hamilton East as it is in the Revised Statutes is made impossible to' be understood. According to the statute Hamilton East consists of wards 1, 6 and 7. There is another ward added now, and wards 1, 6, 7 and 8 constitute Hamilton East; but ward 7 as it is referred to in the statute no longer exists; it has been cut in two, and one-half of the old ward 7 remains as ward 7. The other half of ward 7 and the new district from the_ country now constitute ward 8. According to the reading of the statute, all of ward 8 is out of Hamilton East. Then, a part of ward 7 having been put into ward 8, the people so removed into ward 8 are probably disfranchised. When I called the attention of the Secretary of State to this matter before Christmas, the answer I got from him was that there would be a redistribution before another election, and, therefore, no immediate legislation was necessary. I understand that the position is somewhat reversed to-day, and that we are likely to have an election before a redistribution, and, therefore, I think the matter should
receive the attention of the government, because it may cause a serious difficulty in the three districts-the county of Wentworth and the two Hamiltons.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ELECTIONS IN NORTHERN ONTARIO.
speechtext: I would like to know exactly what my hon. friend means. The ridings of Hamilton have been settled and decided by legislation of this parliament, As I understand, the new legislation to which he refers is legislation of the province of Ontario, and I do not see what effect it can have upon our own definition of our own ridings.

maintopic: ELECTIONS IN NORTHERN ONTARIO.
speechtext: The Revised Statutes simply declare that wards 1, 6 and 7 under the laws of Ontario constitute Hamilton East.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ELECTIONS IN NORTHERN ONTARIO.
speechtext: As they then existed.

maintopic: ELECTIONS IN NORTHERN ONTARIO.
speechtext: Ward 7 is not at all the same area that it was in 1906. Then where is ward 8?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ELECTIONS IN NORTHERN ONTARIO.
speechtext: They are exactly where they were when our statutes were passed. They cannot be changed by any legislation of Ontario.

maintopic: ELECTIONS IN NORTHERN ONTARIO.
speechtext: I doubt that very much, and there is a great difference of opinion upon it. When in 1907 changes were made in the districts of Alberta and Saskatchewan this government immediately passed an Act amending the Revised Statutes in regard to thoise districts. Our statute speaks of ward 7, not as having particular dimensions, but as ward 7. Read that statute to-day, a statute is read as now speaking, and it refers to ward 7 as ward 7 is. I take it, that would be the legal effect of it, and ward 7 now omits a large portion of what was ward 7 in 1906. That portion, together with an addition from the county, is now ward 8. Those people from the county are not assessed in the county of Wentworth, and cannot take the oath as being residents of that country, because they 'are residents of Hamilton. I submit, with all respect to the right hon. gentleman, that therp is great need of making this matter _ perfectly clear so that there will be no dispute as to what those constituencies consist of.

maintopic: ELECTIONS IN NORTHERN ONTARIO.
speechtext: In that particular case, who would be authorized to divide the voters in that portion of the city which was originally in the county of Wentworth? The Act provides that it shall be done by the municipal authorities. Who would be authorized to divide the voters and establish the new polling subdivisions?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ELECTIONS IN NORTHERN ONTARIO.
speechtext:
But for the authority of my hon. friend from Hamilton, who is a legal light, and for whose judgment I have great respect, I should say

that there is no question at all in this matter that the riding of Hamilton or West Hamilton to-day exists just as it existed when the statute was passed in 1906.

maintopic: ELECTIONS IN NORTHERN ONTARIO.
speechtext: I have had considerable experience in the matter, and I must agree with the right hon. the Prime Minister. The impression has been in the ridings _ I have been interested in that the riding is, what it was on the day the statute was passed and it has been left to the returning officer in conjunction with one of the government officials to divide up the voters lists.

speakerposition: topic
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE IMPERIAL CONFERENCE.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Mr FIELDING moved that the House go into committee of Ways and Means.

speakerposition: subtopic
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE IMPERIAL CONFERENCE.
speechtext: ['If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Boyce) reiterates in .spite of what I said that I attempted to mislead the House, I have only to give that statement an unqualified denial.']

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE IMPERIAL CONFERENCE.
speechtext:
I regret to intrude upon the discussion of matter which appears to be not yet exhausted, but I think I am justified in presenting to the House the motion which I have in my hand respecting another matter not less important- a matter which I think deserves the immediate consideration of the House.
Hon. members will recollect that not many weeks ago we adjourned for the purpose of allowing my right hon. friend the Prime Minister to attend two very important functions in England, the Coronation of His Majesty King George and the Imperial Conference. I think the House agreed unanimously that it was absolutely necessary to suspend work here, and permit my right hon. friend and his two colleagues, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Brodeur) and. the Minister of Militia (Mr. Borden) to attend these functions. That conference has taken place and decisions of the utmost importance to our country have been arrived at, . As the House is aware the policy of the Dominion is largely directed according to the decisions arrived at by our ministers attending these conferences. It seems to me this alone would be a sufficient reason to justify us in knowing what proceedings took iplace .at the conference and what decisions were arrived at. I will even go so far as to say that I think it would be out of place for an assembly such as ours, not to show some solicitude under the circumstances as to exactly what conclusions were arrived at by the conference. If the presence of our ministers was absolutely necessary there, if numerous decisions were arrived at on questions which greatly affect the future policy of this country, it seems to me that these ministers should be anxious to place before the House the result of what transpired during the sittings of this conference. Delegates to a meeting of this kind act under ministerial responsibility. They are responsible to the House Sir WILFRID LAURIER
for the opinions they give at these gatherings, and for the votes they cast. Under the circumstances I think it behooves them, upon their return, to give the House a full, complete and sincere account of all the transactions of the meeting.
There has been an impression existing that the meetings of the conference are private. That is not by any means correct. It is sufficient to refer to the precis of the meetings of the conference, which was placed before the British House of Commons last June, to see that that is not the decision of the conference. The question of the procedure at the meeting came up for decision on March 23rd, and the proceedings of the conference on the point will be found at page 10 o<f the precis. It was decided that the deliberations would be private but the decisions would be published. As a matter of fact the decisions were communicated to the public press, and formed the basis of this precis, which contains many subjects of great interest to the House of Commons, and it is a matter of surprise to me that my right hon. friend and his colleagues have not found it possible to lay a similar resume before this House. There is no valid reason, so far as I can see, why we should not have had such a resume and a report of the proceedings of the conference. My right hon friend the Prime Minister admitted in this House the other day that we were entitled to have such a report, and told us that we would have it shortly. Hon. members will find in this precis numerous decisions concerning the declaration of London-a point of controversy most interesting to ourselves and to the entire British Empire. It also contains the decisions of the conference in reference to 35 or 40 other subjects of general interest. However, what I wish to point out to the House is that the precis in question throws no light whatever on naval or military matters. There is not a man in this House who will deny that these are matters of the most vital importance, or that they have been the subject of acute controversy throughout the country since the Imperial Conference on defence held in 1909. The matter was discussed at that conference and at the subsidiary conference held during the summer of 1909, and a new policy was agreed upon; yet there is scarcely any allusion to the important decisions arrived at upon these matters. The reason for the withholding of this information appears to be that military matters and naval matters were deliberated upon in the Conference of Imperial Defence, sitting apart from the conference, but there is proof abundant that the decisions of that committee were brought before the conference, submitted to it and approved by it.
Let me briefly refer to these allusions. At page 11, the president, the right hon.

Prime Minister (Mr. Asquith) in defining the procedure to be adopted at the conference gave indications of how the proceedings would be had in regard to these important matters:
Mr. Asquith explained that naval and military matters would be discussed in the Committee of Imperial Defence where they would have the advantage of the presence of experts. Certain other technical matters it would probably he found desirable not to bring before the conference until after preliminary discussion by the representatives of the Dominion governments interested with the departments of His Majesty's government immediately concerned.
Then there is a short reference, at page 79, to the reports of the committee on defence. It is stated that:
The conference received and approved the report of the committee on Military Imperial Defence, which had held two sittings in the War Office under the chairmanship of the chief of the general staff.
Finally, closing the proceedings, the right hon. Prime Minister, president of the conference spoke as follows:
So again our discussions, conducted also and necessarily under the same veil of confidence in regard to co-operation for naval and mill-tary purposes, have resulted, I think, in a most satisfactory agreement, which, while it recognizes our common obligations, at the same time acknowledges with equal clearness that those obligations must be performed in the different parts of the empire in accordance with the requirements of local opinion and local need and local circumstances.
Now, what I submit to this House is that there is no possible question as to the right and propriety of parliament to be informed on military and naval agreements which may have modified in some respects- in important respects-the agreements arrived at in 1909, and which have been communicated, as properly they should be, to this House. Surely, the right, the absolute necessity, of parliament being informed of these decisions and agreements cannot be called in question. We have the control of our own military matters; we furnish the money with which the whole militia of this country is maintained; what navy it is proposed we shall have is to be built with the people of Canada's money: and it seems to me there can be no possible reason for refusing to this House the full details of the agreements and arrangements made at this conference which will be the foundation of the policy of this country in respect of these two most important matters. It would not be pretended for a moment, I suppose, that these matters fall into the category of war secrets, of state affairs; that they are to be assimilated to undisclosed plans of mobilization on sea or land, plans of foTtifica- 1 tions or any of these matters which under 1
common agreement, under the law of every country are kept absolutely secret. These are agreements of a public nature, given over to the people of the great British dependencies, discussed in their parliaments; and surely nobody will pretend that we are to be refused communication of these decisions arrived at, for instance, on status with regard to the Imperial Admiralty authorities. But the conduct of my right hon. friend and his friends indicates that they have that intention; and I wish, for my part, to know if the House will uphold them in carrying out that intention.
The arrival of my right hon. friend and his colleagues returning from the conference was heralded throughout the ministerial press of this country, and details were given as to what had been transacted at that conference. Indeed, long before the conference was ended, the Ministerial press and other newspapers handed out to the public information respecting the decisions of the conference, which, under the circumstances, it seems to me, it is our right to have corrected. We have the right too to have before parliament the decisions arrived at on the matters laid before that important gathering. As early as the 26th of May, the 'Montreal Herald,' the official organ of the government in Montreal, said:
The difficult problems of the immediate authority of generals and imperial admirals, upon the armies and navies of the empire in time of war.	,
Surely, if that question has been solved at the conference, we are entitled to know in what sense it has been solved.	A
despatch appearing in the 'Star' of the 15th of June, stated that at Pontypool in England, the right hon. the First Lord of the Admiralty, Mr. McKenna, .stated that at that conference 'most satisfactory arrangements had been concluded between the colonies and the British government, and that the dominions had united in order to furnish and maintain the necessary means of defence.
But it is in the ministerial press of this country more particularly that we have an interpretation beforehand of what was done at the conference, and in a sense, I submit to the House, at absolute variance to what is disclosed by this short precis which has reached us since the conference. Let me give some idea to the House of how public opinion, at any rate in my own province, and I think very much in the same way everywhere, has been instructed in regard to the decisions of the conference. Just as my right hon. friend arrived, a special souvenir album was published in the city of Montreal, giving to the public the transactions of the conference, and bestowing unstinted praise upon my right hon. friend because, at the

1010S
conference, and so to speak alone, he withstood all those who were inclined to imperial confederation, those who would attack the autonomy of the dependencies. This article was reproduced with approval on the 13th of July, by ' Le Canada.' in Montreal, the ministerial organ. Let me give to the House some samples of the statements that are made there, and I think when the House reads these statements which have never been controverted in any way by the right hon. gentleman, they will agree that we are entitled to have the true version of what took place at that gathering. I will now read from ' Le Canada
Upon the occasion of the return of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, a souvenir album has been issued which contains a substantial article upon the work and career of the Prime Minister. We reproduce the following:
This popular ovation is but the just return for the work accomplished by Sir Wilfrid Laurier during his entire political life, and which he has just magnificently crowned at London, of work of harmony, of peace and of progress.
Speaking of one of the proposals made at the conference, the paper says:
Another proposal which at first sight seemed most attractive hut in reality was fraught with danger, well understood by Sir Wilfrid, was the suggestion that the Imperial government should consult the dominions upon its foreign policy. . . A painful and even perilous situation which Sir Wilfrid, ever solicitous of the minutest particle of our perfect autonomy, wished to preserve us against, and he succeeded as well as on the preceding occasions.
Does my right hon. friend find this report exact and correct? The precis shows us that my right hon. friend took at the conference an absolutely different position from that which is laid to his credit in these lines of his own newspaper. Does he not admit that under those circumstances we are entitled to have the true version of the proceedings at that gathering? My right hon. friend knows perfectly well, in the first place, that no attempt was made, so far at least as the precis shows, to invade our autonomy. My right hon. friend did not on any occasion stand alone, and he acquiesced absolutely in a proposal under which a consultation of the Dominions should take place. Does my right hon. friend deny that? He admits it. How then can he take unto himself, as he is given in this newspaper, and in many other in our own province, credit for having withstood the adoption of a proposal which he himself acceded to very williingly? Continuing ' Le Canada ' says:
We now come to the naval questions discussed at the conference. These questions have for us a lively interest, inasmuch as they permit us to better appreciate in what spirit the Canadian navy was created.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE IMPERIAL CONFERENCE.
speechtext:
If that is a question of a lively interest for us why should the conclusions of the conference be withheld from us? Why should they not be given to us at once, as I maintain that the government should give them to us? The paper continues:
At a preceding conference, a discussion took place as to the share which each dominion would take in general defence. Canadian representatives had objected to every proposal of direct contribution, and, in general way to any control exercised by the metropolis on the Canadian parliament which must remain, according to them, masters and free to decide in the matter.
The Canadian parliament, in 1910, approved of the creation of a naval service as the best and only means of contributing to the general defence without breaking local autonomy, that is to say, to take unto the charge of Canada gradually, the defence of its own territory. It is in this very sense that the government presented its Naval Bill, that parliament adopted it by its Liberal majority, that Liberal speakers and the Liberal press favourable to the project explained it to the people.
Shameless adversaries, desirous to gain some party advantage upon a question so near to the nation's heart have tried to falsify the meaning of the measure, some using it as a proof of disloyalty and treason, others in denouncing it as imperalism and death to our race. These dishonest and blind talkers have now exhausted their prose and comments; the people, a moment disturbed by their noise, now knows the matter in its conception and principle. They know that the government has not deceived them. Their last doubts have vanished during this conference of 1911, wherein the autonomous character of our navy has been marked in indelible manner.
In order to set at rest all question as to the freedom of action of our navy and the control which we intend exercising upon it, Sir Wilfrid has established a free maritime zone both on the Atlantic and the Pacific, which zone shall be absolutely under our care.
In this is the confirmation authentic, definite and unanswerable of our autonomy in regard to our navy.
There was also the question of the flags. What will be our naval flag? It was strictly necessary in order to accredit us in the different seas of the world, and with foreign countries that we should carry the ensign of the English navy:
Canada, whilst gradually conquering the attributes of a nation, is not yet quite, in the eyes of other countries, an independent nation. But while maintaining its character of a British possession, Canada will hoist its flag upon its navy.
The Canadian navy will use, at the same time, the white ensign which will procure for its ships the freedom of all the seas, and the flag with the Canadian arms. In the British navy, there are the White Ensign and the Union Jack; in the Canadian navy the latter will be replaced by a flag with our arms.
The drift of these decisions is obvious; they settle the field of action of our navy, and the flag which must be unfurled at our masthead.

It affirms our autonomy and the perfect cou-trol which we exercise over it. . .

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE IMPERIAL CONFERENCE.
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman allow me a question? Is the hon. member opposed to the attitude taken by the right hon. the leader of the government before the Imperial Conference?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE IMPERIAL CONFERENCE.
speechtext: If my hon. friend (Mr. Devlin) will give me the decisions arrived at by that conference, I will say what I think of the attitude of the right hon. gentleman. I am sorry that my hon. friend does not quite understand the gist of my argument.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE IMPERIAL CONFERENCE.
speechtext: If the hon. member declares he is not a dissentient, what is he objecting to in connection with the attitude of the Prime Minister?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE IMPERIAL CONFERENCE.
speechtext: Objecing to nothing; 1 am asking for something that I know the House will sanction and it is a reasonable and legitimate demand. I am not going for a single moment to discuss the merits of the question.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE IMPERIAL CONFERENCE.
speechtext: If the attitude of the Prime Minister is such as has been declared in the press is the hon. gentleman in favour of it?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE IMPERIAL CONFERENCE.
speechtext: Well, that is a hypothetical question. It seems to me that we have held sufficient public meetings in Quebec, to many of which I saw my hon. friend come as a spectator, to enable him to know what our opinion is.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE IMPERIAL CONFERENCE.
speechtext: Answer, answer.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE IMPERIAL CONFERENCE.
speechtext:
Without discussing the merits of the question, will anybody deny having regard to the justice of what I am claiming we should be refused fo'r a single moment information as to the decisions arrived at by the conference upon these two very important points? We know what was the decision arrived at with regard to naval matters in 1909. The right hon. gentleman told us, when he introduced the Naval Bill, that the object he had in view was to carry out the policy of the conference of 1909. Surely, when a conference has been held since and these matters have been touched upon, when we are told that a further solution has been arrived at, we are entitled at this moment and under these circumstances, on the eve of a dissolution of this House, when it is in the power of these hon. gentlemen to give it to us, to have this report upon these questions. We have stated time and again upon every occasion in the meetings we have held in our province that we were prepared upon all these questions to accept the verdict of the people of this country. What we claimed was that the people were entitled to such a consultation. No position could be franker, could be fairer and in face of
the calumnious statements which have been circulated, I think it necessary to recall the attitude to which we have constantly adhered. I believe that we have in the past received the support of those who sit around me here upon this side of the House in our insistence upon the right of the people to pronounce upon these questions. Will the right hon. gentleman state in the House that it was not possible for him to lay that report before the House upon his arrival? Were not the proceedings of the conference taken down as ,its sittings proceeded? Did Sir Wilfrid Laurier state to the House the other day that he had taken any step whatever to procure that report for communication to our parliament?	In answer to the last
question I put to the right hon. gentleman on this subject, he said in a scoffing manner that I knew as much about it as he did himself. If the right hon. gentleman today, when these proceedings have been fully transcribed, cabled to have them, we could have them here and have a copy laid before the House before the adjournment. Will the right hon. gentleman deny that? We could have them within a week and they could be laid before the House. The right hon. gentleman stated the other day that as far as he knew they were on the way out. The right hon. gentleman seems to have lost consciousness of the fact that the House unanimously adjourned in order that he should represent us at that important gathering. Nothing whatever in his conduct shows that he took any steps whatever to bring to us a report of what he did there. He returned to the House, took his seat in this House, he gave no statement whatever of what had been done at that conference, and he only learned from those members sititing on our own side that the precis had arrived. I am loth to believe that the two ministers most directly interested, the hon. Minister of Militia and Defence (Sir Frederick Borden) and the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Brodeur) have come back without notes of what was decided with regard to their own departments. Every day the proceedings were written up and placed in the hands of the delegates. Why should we not have the decisions arrived at in regard to those zones. We are going to be called upon in a few days, to vote the beginning of vast sums of money for naval purposes. Will the right hon. gentleman pretend that these definitions of zones are private matters? The House is aware that it was an open question for over twenty years in the important dependency of Australia. First, the delimitations of the zones were fixed for the Commonwealth of Australia and a subscription of, I think 1100,000 sterling was granted. That zone was continued for some years then it was altered, the amount of the sub-

scription was 'altered and then the zone was altered again. There never was any thought at any time that this was a secret matter; it was laid before the parliament of this dependency and was discussed, everything was published and above board. Why should not we be made aware of the decisions which were arrived at upon these subjects, when it is absolutely in the power of the government to give us this report and when we are entitled to it? I therefore move:
That all the words after the word * that ' in the main motion he erased and replaced by the following:
That in the opinion of this House a complete report of the proceedings of the Imperial Conference of 1911 should be communicate!! to parliament forthwith.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE IMPERIAL CONFERENCE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, to a great many of the propositions which have been asserted by my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) 1 have no exception at all to take. In many statements which he has made I altogether concur. With the statement which he has made that the House is entitled to be apprised of what took place at the conference I altogether agree. With the statement which he made that myself and my colleagues, when we represented Canada at the conference, acted upon our ministerial responsibility, I also altogether agree. My action is not to-day before the House. It will be, I hope, before many days. The report of the conference will be placed not only before this House but before the Canadian people and then it will be open to the criticism of every one of His Majesty's subjects in this country. I may say to my hon. friend that I have no intention whatever of shirking the responsibility which I incurred on that occasion. The duties with which I was entrusted, I discharged to the best of my ability and judgment and so did my colleague. My action may command the approval of some; it may suggest the criticism of others. That is incidental to the duties which I had to discharge upon that occasion and to the duty which I have to discharge whenever I act in my present capacity.
And, therefore, upon this occasion my hon. friend has laid down a principle which lies at the base of parliamentary government. He only finds fault with me because the proceedings of the conference have not been laid before parliament. The objection of my hon. friend would have greater force if he could say that the Canadian Ministers who had attended the conference had been in any way derelict in the duty they owe to parliament in this respect. If the report of the conference had been placed' before the Imperial House of Commons, and not before this House, my hon. friend would Mr. MONK.
have legitimate cause for complaint, but, Sir, the fact is that at this moment I have no reason to believe that the report has yet been placed before'the Imperial parliament so surely no one in this House can blame this government because the report has not been placed on the table of this House.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE IMPERIAL CONFERENCE.
speechtext: I would blame tire government if it had been given to the newspapers instead of to this House.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE IMPERIAL CONFERENCE.
speechtext: What newspapers have got the report? Here is the report which has been obtained by the newspapers, it is the precis and nothing else.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE IMPERIAL CONFERENCE.
speechtext: Is our obtaining the report of the conference contingent upon its being laid before the British parliament?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE IMPERIAL CONFERENCE.
speechtext:
My hon. friend and every member will expect that the full report of the conference will be placed before all the parliaments represented at that conference. The organization of the conference was under the control of the Secretary of State for the Colonies, and the officers of the Colonial Office were the secretaries of the conference; it was they who prepared the precis to which my hon. friend has alluded and who were charged with preparing the full report. At page 78 of the precis will be found the report of the sitting of June 20.
The conference discussed the question of the publication of the proceedings and decided they should be published at as early date as possible.
The publication of these proceedings was entrusted not to the representatives of Canada or any other Dominion, but to the officers of the Colonial Office.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE IMPERIAL CONFERENCE.
speechtext: Are we dependent for that report of the conference upon what may be done at the Colonial Office? Have we not an inherent right to these proceedings?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE IMPERIAL CONFERENCE.
speechtext: My hon. friend surprises me. Somebody must do that clerical work.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE IMPERIAL CONFERENCE.
speechtext: Where did the newspapers get the report?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE IMPERIAL CONFERENCE.
speechtext: I am sure I cannot answer that question, they did not get it from me.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE IMPERIAL CONFERENCE.
speechtext: The precis was made and published in London, it was distributed among the press.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE IMPERIAL CONFERENCE.
speechtext:
The other day my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) brought to the attention of the House a statement that the proceedings of i- the conference had been placed before the

Imperial parliament. I was surprised at this, but it turned out that it was the precis which had been placed before the British House of Commons.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE IMPERIAL CONFERENCE.
speechtext: Who prepared that?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE IMPERIAL CONFERENCE.
speechtext: Mr. Just, now Sir Arthur Just.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE IMPERIAL CONFERENCE.
speechtext: Was he an official at the conference?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE IMPERIAL CONFERENCE.
speechtext: An official of the Colonial Office, and placed in charge of the reporting of the proceedings by the Secretary of State for the Colonies. He prepared the precis which was given to the press every day, and which has now been published in book form. My hon. friend (Mr. Monk), is anxious to have not only this partial report, but the full report of the proceedings. His motion specifically calls for the full report, and I have read the decision of the conference to have that full report published at as early a date as possible. It is not my business or the business of my colleagues who were at the conference with me to arrange for the publication of that report.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE IMPERIAL CONFERENCE.
speechtext: It is his business to see that equal treatment is accorded to Canada and the other portions of the empire in the distribution of that report.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE IMPERIAL CONFERENCE.
speechtext: That is exactly what I say, that if there had been any dereliction on our part hon. gentlemen would have a right to complain, but nothing of that kind has taken place.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE IMPERIAL CONFERENCE.
speechtext: Do I understand that we must wait until the report is placed on the table of the Imperial House?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE IMPERIAL CONFERENCE.
WAYS AND MEANS-THE IMPERIAL CONFERENCE.
speechtext: You won't give us what we want.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE IMPERIAL CONFERENCE.
speechtext: This is not the time nor the occasion to discuss the question, but the time will not be long coming, I hope, and it will come sooner than my hon. friend wants. My hon. friend has not waited for the report to discuss it He has discussed it, and has condemned my course. This is not the time to discuss this question; but, Sir, I appeal to the fairness and the common sense of men on both sides of this House. Here is a motion in the form of a motion of want of_confidence, asking the House to censure us-for what? Because we have not put upon the table of the House a report which we have not, a report which has not yet been placed upon the table of the House of Commons in England so far as I know. I will make inquiry this very day whether it has been or not. If it had been placed on the table of the House of Commons in England, I suppose I would know that, because there would have been a despatch coming to us informing us of the fact.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE IMPERIAL CONFERENCE.
speechtext:
Did my hon. friend cable
for it?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE IMPERIAL CONFERENCE.
speechtext: I did not, but I will. I shall be happy to give that pleasure to my hon. friend. I shall have the pleasure of discussing that report with my hon. friend as soon as it is laid on the table of the House, and the sooner it comes the better for myself. But, I ask, has there been any undue delay in the matter on the part of the government? Who is to blame because this report is not on the table of the House? Is the Canadian House of Commons entitled to greater privilege than the Imperial House of Commons?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE IMPERIAL CONFERENCE.
speechtext: We are entitled to exactly the same privilege.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE IMPERIAL CONFERENCE.
speechtext: Exactly-what I say also; and when the report is placed on the table of the Imperial House of Commons, if it is not placed on the table of this House, then my hon friend will have reason to complain, but not till then.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE IMPERIAL CONFERENCE.
speechtext:
I entirely agree with the Prime Minister that the attitude



of the government at the conference ought to be discussed with full information as to what did take place. I am not at all advised as to the differences which may make themselves manifest when we have the full report as distinguished from the precis. It may be that they will be important, though I would not have supposed they would be, because otherwise the precis itself would be misleading. I think it would be advisable in the meantime that the precis itself, which has been received, should be placed on the table of the House and become a part of the records of this parliament; and, as I understand, there is no objection to that.
Now, reference has been made to newspaper 'Comments. I do not propose to go into the merits of those comments, for the reason that I have already indicated. But I think it is a matter of some concern to this parliament as to whether or not certain reports of what was done at the conference, *which have appeared in the organs of the right hon. gentleman, have any foundation in fact or not. The right hon. gentleman says he did not communicate that information to those organs. It is perfectly manifest that they must have obtained the information either from himself or from some of his colleagues, because there was no one else to give it. There has been a good deal of reference to zones established on both the Atlantic and Pacific, and I think it is legitimate comment that the information in regard to those zones appears in the party press under the control of the right hon. gentleman, though it is not laid before parliament, and that its appearance in that press is for the purpose of assisting a political campaign on his behalf. I submit that that is not a fair use for any minister of the Crown to make of his position and of the confidential information which is given to him. I say that any member of that conference who uses his confidential position for the purpose of imparting to his party press confidential information of that kind for the purposes of a political campaign is not worthy of the position he occupies.
As far as the rest of it is concerned, I do not propose to deal with the question upon its merits, for the reason the Prime Minister has stated, that there may be important differences between the report which we have now and the full report which is to come later. We once more see the Prime Minister, according to his party press, in the well-recognized, but rather threadbare garb of the saviour of the autonomy of Canada. It is impossible for the right hon. gentleman to cross the Atlantic without saving the autonomy of Canada. He has been there in 1897, in 1902, and in 1907, and on every one of those occasions he came back after having saved the autonomy of this country.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE IMPERIAL CONFERENCE.
WAYS AND MEANS-THE IMPERIAL CONFERENCE.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE IMPERIAL CONFERENCE.
speechtext: It did not make any difference whether Balfour and Chamberlain were there, or whether Asquith and Haldane were there; it did not matter whether Selborne, Tweedmouth or McKenna were there; every one of these men was ready to destroy the autonomy of this country. That is the position that is cheered by hon. gentlemen opposite. If we are to believe these organs, Premier Asquith, Mr. Haldane, Sir Edward Grey, and all the other British statesmen at the recent conference were conspiring to destroy the autonomy of Canada, and the right hon. gentleman saved it; and the cheers which came from hon. gentlemen opposite just now indicate the character of the campaign which they propose to make. Well, Mr. Speaker, perhaps we had better have a little information later on as to what the assault was which Mr. Asquith, the great Liberal Prime Minister of Great Britain, made on the autonomy of Canada. The Prime Minister will no doubt make us acquainted with that later on.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE IMPERIAL CONFERENCE.
speechtext: Both parties will have seen that Mr. Asquith was saving the autonomy of Canada.	[DOT]

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE IMPERIAL CONFERENCE.
speechtext:
Then the right hon. gentleman should rebuke his supporters, because just now they cheered to the echo the statement that Mr. Asquith, the Liberal Prime Minister of Great Britain had been engaged in a conspiracy to destroy the autonomy of this country. Not only did the supporters of my "right hon. friend cheer this statement, but a member of the government, the Solicitor General (Mr. Bureau) also wildly cheered it. I suppose Mr. Haldane, Mr. Lloyd George, Mr. Winston Churchill and the other distinguished members of the British government were all concerned in this awful conspiracy from which the right hon. gentleman with his sword 'and his shield, and his white plume saved the autonomy of Canada.
I have got down as far as 1907, and on every one of these occasions the autonomy of Canada has been preserved by the Prime Minister. It must be pretty well preserved -iso much so that I think it might foe put away in cold storage for a while, so far as debate is concerned. In 1909 the right hon. gentleman did .not personally pave thd autonomy of Canada, but he did it toy deputy. He deputed my hon. friend the Minister of Militia (Sir Frederick Borden), and my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Brodeur); and the autonomy of Canada was saved by deputy, and not by the right hon. gentleman in person. In 1911 the right hon. gentleman- was again to the tore, and I would think that my hon. friends opposite would

be grateful to us on this side of the House, because, as every one in this country knows, the right hon. gentleman did not intend to go, and did not want to go, and ' would not have gone had it not been for the offer that was made from this side of the House. So, so far as the efforts of thought hon. gentleman on this occasion are concerned, the opposition may be regarded as the direct and proximate cause of the saving of Canada. Perhaps this particular cry has about survived the usefulness which it has served on so many occasions. At all events, when we get the information which the right hon. gentleman promised us we shall learn what was the real character of the bloodthirsty assaults upon the autonomy of Canada made by the Prime Minister of Great Britain and his colleagues.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE IMPERIAL CONFERENCE.
speechtext:
I have before me the London ' Times ' of Saturday July 15, which deals with the Imperial Conference report. In it I find the following:
The issue yesterday afternoon of the minutes of proceedings of the Imperial Conference. 1911 (cd. 5745) come opportunely, before the conference itself has passed from memory, and when the last overseas member of it lias only just left our shores, to remind us of the great issues debated in it, and the real work it accomplished tow ards the knitting together of the empire. The blue book contains a verbatim report of the proceedings of the conference, which have hitherto been published only in the condensed form of the official precis; but as was expected, it includes no record of the joint session of the conference and the committee of defence.
This blue-book was issued in London on July 15th, eleven days ago, and contains a, verbatim report of the proceedings. Yet, Canada is not in possession of that blue-book to day; and, so far as the right hon. gentleman is concerned, he has never seen it. Now, there should have been equal treatment meted out to Canada in that respect, and if London was supplied with copies of that blue-book, why was not an arrangement made whereby a certain number of them should be sent over here?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE IMPERIAL CONFERENCE.
speechtext: If the report has been placed upon the table of the House, I have no doubt it is now on its way here.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE IMPERIAL CONFERENCE.
speechtext:
It was placed on the table in London on the 15th July, eleven days ago. There is a two column summary of the blue-book in this article, and hon. gentlemen can derive a good deal of information as to how much progress was made in the direction of imperial unity at that conference by reading this summary. This progress may have been made with the aid of the right hon. gentleman- perhaps it was made in spite of him. Any way the reading of these proceedings is 3194
satisfactory, and notwithstanding what was done to disturb the unity of that conference and to prevent its drawing the empire together, it was a most successful conference, according to this report, and it shows in what direction the empire is reeving.
The other day the hon. Postmaster General referred to what had taken place in this conference in regard to state ownership of telegraphs and cables, but I am not able to find in the summary of that report that the representatives of Canada at that conference joined with the representatives of Australia in favour of public ownership of cables and telegraphs. If they had done so perhaps we would have had it. It was probably because we had as representatives there, men who were more or less reactionary that a decision was not reached in favour o'f state ownership of cables.
In order that the House may have full information as to what took place there, I propose to read part of the summary of the minutes of proceedings of the Imperial Conference:

speakerposition: subtopic
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE IMPERIAL CONFERENCE.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
On June 15 and 16 the conference devoted itself mainly to considering proposals for the improvement of communications between the various parts of tbe empire. In this Australia and New Zealand, as farthest from the centre, were especially concerned, and were agreed on one point-that communication by cable should be made less difficult and less expensive. Since an improvement in this direction had been made ten years ago by tbe laying of a state-owned cable across the Pacific (which lowered rates to Australia by nearly 40 per cent), it was natural to suggest that a similar state owned cable across the Atlantic would produce a similar effect.
A state-owned cable across the Atlantic would reduce telegraph rates by 40 per cent, yet, so far as I know the representatives of Canada did not insist on that proposal being carried out nor on the state-owned cable across the Atlantic being constructed by Canada by Great Britain or by the United States jointly. When the hon. Postmaster General gave us his account of the proceedings the other day, he did not give us all the facts because I find:
The British Postmaster General, however, brought forward another plan, depending partly on negotiations with the private companies that own existing cables-such as, he pointed out, are already securing a 50 per cent reduction in the cost of uncoded messages: partly on the establishment of effective government control over rates charged on lines which land on British territory. The Australasian representatives were still inclined to press for a state-owned cable, but were persuaded by the other members of the conference to accept a compromise whereby, if Mr. Samuel's methods did not secure consid

speakerposition: subtopic
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE IMPERIAL CONFERENCE.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
erable reductions, the state-owned cable could still be advocated at a subsidiary conference.
My contention is this-if the representatives of Canada had backed up the representatives of Australia we would have had state owned cables on the Atlantic, and a resulting reduction of 40 per cent in the cost of cable messages.
In order to show how much progress has been made I would like to read another paragraph relating to the results of the conference.
But these somewhat ineffective discussions were immediately followed by a striking demonstration of the empire's real unity. For three days the overseas members of the conference, sitting with the Committee of Imperial Defence, were initiated into the secrets of Britain's foreign policy

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
There is Imperial progress. The representatives of the various overseas dominions, were, for the first time, made parties to the foreign policy of the Empire.
' Hitherto,' said the Australian Prime Minister, at a later date, ' we have been negotiating with the government of the United Kingdom at the portals of the household.'
You have thought it wise. Sir, to take the representatives of the dominions into the inner councils of the nation. . . I think no better step has ever been taken or Can be taken by any responsible advisers of the King. I hope, as I feel, that there will be no going back on that sound principle.
And the summary goes on to say:
It is unnecessary here to dwell on the arrangement of ideas about the empire which must have preceded the taking of this step; but it must exert considerable influence both on the status of Dominion cabinets and on the scope of their discussions. No responsible Prime Minister can in future admit among his colleagues men unfit to be the depositaries of imperial secrets, and no oversea cabinet can construct its own policy without considering the effect of it upon the foreign relations of the empire as a whole.
Now, there is the first declaration of the unity of the whole empire, a joining of the empire for purposes of defen ie and the maintenance of the common cause; and that fact alone shows how important that Imperial Conference was, what great results have been attained and what greater results will come in the future when it is better established and there is a better understanding between the different members. Now, when there is so fuLl a summary of these proceedings and when the full report has been published in London, I contend that we in Canada ought to be put in possession of the facts and ougnt to have that official report at the disposal of this House, and this country as soon as they have it in London, less the days it takes to cross the Atlantic. If the 'Tim;s' cm have that report and digest it, and if there Mr. MACLEAN (York).
is time for that newspaper summary to reach us, we are entitled to have the full official report here at the same time. In fact it ought to be here a little before, because it could leave before the ' Times ' got it. But we know nothing about it; the Prime Minister does not even know whether it has been printed. Perhaps the gentlemen in the colonial office still regard Canada as a colony as in the old days of Downing street. It would be a good thing to wake them up and give them to understand that in handing out these documents Canada is not to be forgotten. The way to work that out was for those who represented us in the conference to have made arrangements before the conference separated that copies of the proceedings should be forwarded to this country. And I hold that it is the duty of the Prime Minister to set the cables at work so that this House may be put in possession of this document which was distributed in London eleven days ago.
