WAYS AND MEANS-THE IMPERIAL CONFERENCE.
speechtext:
Before you leave the Chair, I wish to call the attention of the
Hopse to a matter that I referred to on the 14th of last December. It has relation to certain claims that have been advanced by the pioneers of western Canada for the last 38 or 40 years. When I asked the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver) on the 14th of last December as to the correctness of the report that the present government had finally denied all recognition to these claimants, I at that time gave notice that as soon as possible I would bring the matter up. Consequently he will not charge me now with being an obstructionist in carrying out my word. This'is a matter, as I say, that has been more or less under dispute ever since the year 1870, consequently it has all the merits that belong to antiquity. Now the parties for whom I speak are earlier settlers of the Northwest who arrived in that country between the first days of January, 1836, and the 15th of July, 1870. Every one in the House is aware that the Northwest Territories, that is to say, the Red River country, was ceded to confederation on the 15th day of July, 1870. By that cession certain recognition was made to those who had rights of occupancy and possession in the Northwest Territories at that time. Subsequently, on the 26th of May, 1874, the recognition that was made in 1870 was altered, and a more extensive grant was made to those to whom grants had been made before, and to others by the Act 37 Vic., chap. 20. All I need to tell the House is the final result, what recognition was made, who enjoyed it, and what others were left out. In 1813 the Selkirk colony was established. Up to the time that the final settlement was adjusted on the 26th of May, 1874, settlers of many descriptions had secured rights in the Northwest Territories. They comprised five classes. There were the original Selkirk settlers themselves, there were the other British settlers, there were French Canadians, and there were the Indians and the Halfbreeds. As to the latter two classes my remarks have no bearing. There is no complaint as to the recognition by the Dominion of Canada, by what is known in law as an act of grace, of the rights of occupancy of the Halfbreeds and Indians. I will only compare the rights of the Halfbreed children that existed at that time in Manitoba with those on whose behalf I present a case this afternoon. However, as to the first three classes, a settlement was made of a very strange and arbitrary character, that is to say, as to the original Selkirk settlers, the other British settlers not of that class, and the French Canadian settlers, an arbitrary settlement was made with them. A line was drawn at the 1st of January, 1836; as to all who had arrived in the Northwest Territories prior to that time a grant of 160 acres of land was made. In the first place,

when the adjustment was first made in 1872, a grant of only 140 acres was made, and that only to the original Selkirk settlers. But by the amended Act of 1874 a final adjustment was arrived at whereby the original Selkirk settlers, the other British settlers and the French Canadians were subjected to the arbitrary settlement arrived at, those who had arrived prior to the 1st of January, 1836, obtaining a grant of 160 acres, and those who arrived subsequent to that time being utterly ignored. Not only were those who arrived between 1813 and 1836 recognized by the land grant, but their children born prior to the 15th of July, 1870, were also recognized, and they received the same grant; in fact all the lineal descendants then living were entitled under that Act to the same grant as the original settlers. Not only did the Act of the 26th of May, 1874, go that far, but what is more astonishing, it went further, it made exactly the same grant to another class who were not even born at the time the territory was ceded to confederation, namely, to the descendants of the first settlers between 1813 and 1836 who were born between the 15th of July, 1870, and the 26th of May, 1874. So the ultimate result is this, so far as it relates to the British and ' French Canadian settlers, that those who came in at first between 1813 and 1836 and their lineal descendants born up to the 15th of July, 1870, when the territory was ceded, and all born after the cession of the territory prior to the 26th of May, 1870 received from the bounty of confederation this grant of 160 acres. Why the line was drawn I am at a loss to know, why it was fixed there, or fixed at all, I am also at a loss to say. Why it should be that those whose rights of occupancy and possession accrued between 1836' and 1870 should be ignored in the settlement, is at this distance hard to understand. The records of the department, I think, will foe searched in vain for any reason why the arbitrary line was thus drawn, or why any line was drawn.
I venture further to say that the records of -such settlements in other countries will also be searched in vain to establish the principle that any line should be drawn at any period. The rights of occupancy of territory should not be differentiated as to time at all, because all -rights of occupancy are the same for different classes, whether for the early settler or the late arrival. I do not intend to press that argument just at the present stage. I want to outline the state of affairs that has resulted first. The number of claimants is not large. Of the first class, that is those who received recognition, -being actual settlers between 1813 and 1836, the number, according to the Mr. MEIGHEN.
best compiled figures-I presume they are accurate-is 244.	But of their children
and descendants born prior to the 15th July, 1870, the date of the cession, there were 477, and of those who were granted the reward of occupancy, although indeed they were not born at this time, they having been born between the 15th of July, 1870, and the 26t,h of May, 1874, there were 128. So that, summing it all up, it will be seen that to 45 per cent of those who had established rights of occupancy and-possession at the time of the cession, grants were made and to 55 per cent no recognition was given.
This matter has been brought before this and previous governments. It has been a question involving considerable irritation in the west. I wish to trace the efforts^ that have been made to secure recognition, not -so much to bring home a case against the government, but rather to present what appears to me a good argument against what is usually brought forward as establishing the absence of any" right of these present -claimants. The contention of the government, when the case was last presented to them,, -rested on two positions. . The position, first of all, was that the claim is too old-, that it is of forty years standing now, and that -at thi-s stage we cannot review it. They said, secondly, that the policy of the government is thoroughly fixed and final; we shall make no -more land grants except to actual settlers. I do not purpose at this point to criticise the last po-sition. I -aim not asking that the demands of these men, if there is at this -stage a practical objection from that point of view, should be granted in toto, as they present them. W-h-at I argue i-s that some recognition is bound to be made to them before confederation has done its duty to them. What form that shall take or to what extent it shall go,
I do not propose to argue. But I do say that Canada has not discharged her duty towards a clas-s of her citizens, a class which is entitled to, I feel fair in saying, more than ordinary consideration. Why is that the case? When the United States made a settlement of claims under -similar circumstances I know of no in-stance where they did- not recognize rights of occupancy as complete and -deserving of reward even though those rights were established but shortly before the cession. I would refer hon. gentlemen to the Oregon claims when the United States not only recognized the Indian title, not only by way of legal recognition, but also recognized every right of occupancy however brief the period was prior to the cession of the country to the United- States. A right of occupancy is a right that does not depend upon time. A right of possession to a very -great degree

is the same. But, in this particular case there is more than the usual reason why time should not be recognized even in establishing rights of possession as well as rights of occupancy It has never to the best of my knowledge, been recognized in establishing rights of occupancy.
In this case it should not have been allowed t-o interfere as to any rights which many of these old settlers had' of both classes in the matter of a settlement of their claims upon their coming into confederation. Those who arrived in the country at an earlier period were not settlers in the usual sense of the word. They followed the trail, they were mostly employees of the Hudson's Bay Company, in the employ of speculators residing in the old land, and they did not at that time, as history will amply show, have the hardships to endure which subsequently were endured by those who came after them in the west. Between 1836 and 1870 the vanguard of the original Red River colony had to suffer hardships to a greater degree than those who preceded them and they suffered the hardships that are inseparable from early pioneer life. The case on this point is, at least prkna facie, established. No one has yet, be it of this government or of the prior government, ventured to give a logical explanation why the settler who came in 1835 was entitled to recognition and why the settler who came in 1836 was not. No explanation on that point has been ventured, and I understand that the right hon. Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) stated that he himself saw no reason for that. Consequently, on the face of it, the indebtedness is there, the right is there, and the only question is, can we in justice to our country now recognize it, and if we can, then certainly we ought to do it. I can see no reason whatever, in the defence that because the claim is old it must be ignored. It is true that in the law of every civilized nation the principle is established that as claims advance in age they become' less and less deserving of recognition. Our statute of limitations is based upon that principle. The statutes of limitation of every civilized nation are based upon the same principle; that is that a private right that nas been asleep, or dead, on which no claim in court has been made, cannot, after the lapse of stated periods, be advanced with success. Such statutes of limitation are doubtless based upon a sound and necessary principle, namely, that though the duty may Still exist, though the duty still may be owing from one man to his fellow, from one individual to -another, still the danger of enforcing the performance of that duty, the danger of compelling recognition of
the obligation, is so great that it is impossible to insist upon it.
Claims of innocent third parties have come in and, therefore, the dangers of recognizing those claims that have been subject to laches, are -so great as to justify their being ignored. That is the principle of the whole statute of limitations of every country. To that principle I make no dissent. But that principle has no application whatever to the present case; in fact it has always been recognized that in matters of trusteeship there is no statute of limitation that at any time does apply. This is a matter of trusteeship, and consequently on that first principle of general law of this country, and all other countries, there could be no such defence against the claim of the early pioneers of Manitoba, because certainly when this country took over the provinces of the west, when it took over the Red River colony, the Dominion became by that very act trustees for those who had rights of occupaney, and possession in that territory, prior to the "bession, and no trustee can ever get rid of his responsibility to those for whom he is a trustee by pleading the passage of time or any principle of the statute of limitations. That may appear a technical argument. It is not technical, it is in the very nature of the case, it is a necessary principle that we ought at all times to recognize.
The principle on which we are justified in ignoring a claim because it is old is utterly absent in this case. There has been no laches, these men have been doing everything they are called upon to do, ever since they were denied their rights in 1874. They have exercised every diligence to secure their rights, they have been separated by large distances, they have had no common bond but these common grievances, they have bad nothing to bring them together, they have had to present their case with obstacles strewn around them that made it almost impossible, particularly in the early stages of our history, to present any case to a government so far away. But no sooner were they denied their rights in 1870 than their claim was pressed, than an organization was instituted in the west known as the Prince Rupert Pioneers, and that organization, through its representatives in this House and by delegations sent to this parliament, pressed the claim I am now advancing. On what ground did they press it? First of all they based it on the proclamation issued to them by which their consent was obtained to enter confederation ; they based it on the proclamation of the Governor General of that day issued with the authority of Earl Grenville the

Colonial Secretary on the 6th of December, 1879, to the early settlers. In that proclamation it was stated that all such rights would be observed, that all settlers would be treated in the spirit of British justice. That proclamation was supplemented by a further letter on the 16th of February, 1870, by which the Governor General of Canada repeated the same assurance to Bishop TachA I do not mention this to found again any technical right. Had no letter been written, had no assurance been made at all by the government of Great Britain or by this government to the early settlers of that country they would be entitled just the same to the British justice which was assured them by that letter, they would be entitled to a recognition of their right of property. I do not deny that they were partially recognized. Those who had rights of special property, those who had made settlements and had rights defined on special limited properties, were recogniezd, but those who had been in such a line of work, who had been leading such a life that they hacf no defined rights of property, were not recognized, although as a matter of fact they were just as much entitled to the full extent of the letter of the Governor General, they were just as much entitled in a word to their rights of possession and occupancy being recognized as any other class. They were utterly ignored so that I would not rest their claim on any letter of the Governor General nor on any assurance from the home office, but, relying on. the general principles of equal right's on which every section of this country should be able to rely, I state that these men have not been done justice to.
I set about showing that they should not be denied because their claim is old. They petitioned for it in 1871. They had at that time as representative in this House the present High Commissioner for Canada, then Sir Donald A. Smith, and in the ' Hansard ' of 1871 and 1872, will be found utterances by him, representing them, thoroughly coinciding with the claim which they made then and make still demanding that they be recognized in the distribution of this land just the same as the descendants of those who were prior to them. Consequently right at the first, it is clear that they took every step they could take, because not only were they represented and their claim pressed by their representative here, but they actually went to the expense, and a great expense it was to them, of sending a delegation to this parliament also to press their claim. That delegation consisted of Judge Black, Mr. Scott, and Father Riehot. Two of this delegation were not able to return, the other, Father Riehot, did return and made his Teport and in so far as that report, which was Mr. MEIGHEN.
made to the legislative body at that time in existence at Winnipeg, can be found, it shows that while they did not receive a definite promise of the recognition of their claim as presented, it at least has an indication that they were promised recognition at some future day in some form or another, because there is a reference to the fact that when the other provinces of the west were to be annexed at a later time, recognition of those settlers who were outside the Red River colony would be made. Consequently there was to that extent a recognition by the parliament of Canada of the claim of these men.
They did not stop at that. Again in the year 1886 when, of course, another government was in office, further representations were made to this House and in the meantime, not only in 1871 and 1872, but later and up as late as 1886, resolutions were passed unanimously by the provincial legislature sitting at Winnipeg recognizing the rights of these men, and spurning the idea that any. difference existed between their claim at that time, and the claim of those who had already received their grants, and urging that cold justice be done the Red River settlers, and the settlers further west who had arrived between 1836 and 1870. Those resolutions were forwarded to the Governor General in Council at Ottawa, and as a result an investigation was ordered to be made in the Department of the Interior in pursuance of an address from the legislative council of Manitoba which ari'ived on the 8th day of February, 1872. On the 26th of April of the same year an order in council was passed deputing the department to institute an investigation into the claim and to report. The deputy minister, Mr. Burgess, made the investigation and the report.
But I venture to say, with all respect to his memory, that he seems to have misunderstood the purpose of the investigation. He seemed utterly to have misconceived the spirit of the claim which was made against the Dominion of Canada. Mr. Burgess appears to have understood that his mission was to ascertain the legal rights of those settlers, that is to say, whether or not those who had actual legal rights to defined territory at that time had those rights already conceded, or whether there were claims outstanding, and whether or not the parliament of Canada was in a position to resist the claims of the settlers, who arrived between 1866 and 1886. His report bears out the interpretation that I say he put upon his mission. It refers to the care that has always been exercised in the department to see that each claim, as established, was recognized, and it contains these words: Treaty No. 1, of the 3rd of August, 1871, St. Peter s Indian reserve, provides as follows:
' It being understood, however, that if at the

date of the execution of this treaty there are any settlers within the bounds of any land reserved by the band. Her Majesty reserves the right to deal with such settlers _ as she shall deem just, so as not to diminish the extent of land allotted to the Indians.'
Mr. Burgess goes on to say that 'it is difficult to understand exactly what is meant' by the claims of the white settlers after 1835, and he goes on to quote the Acts of 1873 and 1874, and concludes by saying: ,
There never was any other legal provision for making any grant of scrip or land to settlers going into the country subsequent to 1835, except the provisions contained in the_ Manitoba Act for quieting the title of those in possession at the time of the transfer; nor do I find any record in the department of any claim having been advanced or any other compensation than that provided for by the Manitoba Act.
Certainly he would not. No claim could be made legally on the department for any specific land unless it was specified with defined rights of occupancy. These are claims based on another principle altogether, namely, that those whose Tights of occupation did not Tefer to particular lands at the time of the cession were just as much entitled to lands at the time of the cession as those who had particular lands. That Mr. Burgess seems to have missed. He further goes on to say that if an investigation were made as to the rights of those parties:
Such an inquiry could not fail, in my opinion, to have the effect of disturbing and disquieting the whole population of the province of Manitoba, and casting doubts upon the validity of every title hitherto granted by the Crown to claimants under the Manitoba Act.
That further establishes that nothing was done by the investigation of Mr. Burgess to ascertain the rights that these men advanced. How could the title to any lands already granted be affected by a general recognition of the Tight to 160 acres of land or scrip for it? It certainly could not. Those titles already recognized would of course be absolved from it, and they would be in the same position as any others entitled to make a selection just as those before them had done. I am utterly at a loss to understand the objections advanced by Mr. Burgess to the granting of this Tequest. Well, the agitation continued to be kept up, and it was pressed with renewed vigour in 1905 and 1906. The reason of the agitation taking on renewed strength at that time was that those people relied on what they had already long considered-the original promise of the government that when the new territories were made into provinces those rights which at that time were ignored would be at last recognized. The territories were made into provinces in
1905, and from that time on a considerable body of settlers made the demand that their rights be recognized the same as those who had come earlier. Consequently the claim is utterly without foundation that the mere length of time that had elapsed since the original settlement was arrived at puts the matter past the stage of inquiry. In the first place, as I have stated, it falls because there is a trusteeship existing between the government and the people of Canada and those early settlers whose rights of possession and occupancy at least were not reoogniezd by the settlement of July, 1870, and that that trusteeship exists absolutely puts it out of power to plead the lapse of time. Furthermore, it falls because the principle on which it stands does not exist in this case, namely, that they should have earlier pressed their claims to obtain recognition. Ever since the claims were advanced they have been pressed with as much persistency as we could expect under the difficult circumstances in which the settlers were placed. So that it cannot be maintained that we are entitled to ignore their claims simply because 30 or 40 years have elapsed. Further, it cannot be argued, because there is a considerable body of evidence to indicate that their rights were actually recognized in 1871, and that they were promised grants at a future stage in the development of Canada. On these grounds it does not lie in the mouth of the government to-day to say to these men: 'You have waited too long; the lapse of 40 years deprives you of any claim; the unwritten law as to limitations shuts you up, and although you may have had a claim originally, although we recognize that you should not have been denied when your fellow-settlers' claims were granted, we say that you are shut out by the mere lapse of time.' If that defense falls, what defense is left? How can we justify ourselves for saying to these men: 'It is quite true, you went in there in 1836 and 1837, and up to 1870. You bore the burden and the heat of the day in pushing the frontiers of civilization into that country. You endured the trials and suffered the hardships. You faced the dangers and the perils in order that Manitoba particularly and western Canada in general should reach the state of civilization which she has at present attained. You ceded your country under the distinct promise that you would get ample justice, and that all claims of occupancy and possession would be recognized. You came into the contract absolutely entitled to recognition, but we will not recognize you.'
I say unless it can be argued that by virtue of the lapse of time they are not entitled to recognition, there is no ground at all for refusing to recognize them. Now the' government comes and says. 'It is

because in the meantime we have adopted a policy-good though it may be-because in the meantime we have changed the policy of this country, we must refuse to make any land grants and we cannot recognize your claim, however just.' I do not need to spend much time in disposing of that, because it disposes of itself. These men are not to be affected by any change of the policy of Canada, their rights accrued long prior to this change. Although it may interfere with the form of the grant, it cannot interfere with the principle, and it cannot be urged in defence of the policy of non recognition. Their rights, whatever they were, were just the same as were the lights of those who came before them-they were greater than those who were born between 1870 and 1874-they were greater and on a higher plane than many which were recognized, and we cannot say to them now that because we chose to adopt a policy in which we could not grant that recognition in just the same form as we granted it before, we will not grant any recognition at all.
Now, that is the position taken by the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver) as I understand it. The government of this country speaking through the right hon. the Prime Minister and the hon. Minister of the Interior denied recognition to the early settlers who came in between 1836 and 1870. There was no other ground advanced, so far as I can see, and there is no other ground that could be advanced. I argue that it is the duty of the government to ascerain by what means they can give substantial justice to these later arrivals-to these men who stood the greater share of the burden, and who shouldered the greater proportion of the difficulties. This class of men cannot always come to parliament and ask that justice be done them. In the very nature of things they are to-day well advanced in years, and will before long have disappeared from the earth. Many of them are in more or less destitute circumstances. No doubt a good many of them are prosperous, but still some o'f them are in such circumstances as to warrant the government in general taking steps to see that justice is done to them. It is the duty of the government to see without delay if some method cannot be devised whereby the claim of these men will be recognized.

I wish to say a word or two in connection with this matter. I did not know that the question was to come up to day, or I would have had more information to lay before the House. However, there is one case which I would like to bring to the attention of the government. I remember when I was a lad, my nearest neighbour was one o'f the first men who settled in the Red River Mr. METGHEN
district in 1812 and 1813. His name was John Cooper. This man was accused wrongfully of a crime, after he had been long on his land. He was brought to the city of Montreal and kept there in confinement for nearly a year. At the end of this time he proved his innocence and was liberated. He went to work on a building in order that he might earn sufficient money to return to his home in the west. But during the course of his work he fell from the building and when I knew him he had been an invalid *for many years. John Cooper had lived for years-and years on his land where the city of Winnipeg stands to day. He had raised his family there, but after he was taken to Montreal his land was taken from them, and I understand, was sold by the Dominion of Canada. When he carpe to this country, Lord Selkirk promised to give him a deed to certain land, if he would settle on it. He fulfilled his part of the contract, yet the land has been taken from him and his family.
If I cannot do any more for my good old neighbour, I will put on 'Hansard' the story of the injustice which he suffered. We all know that Lord Selkirk in his will left one-tenth of his lands to be given to these settlers. That land extended not only through Manitoba, but all the way up to Fort Carleton, Saskatchewan, and also into the state of Minnesota.
This is a part of Minnesota that the American government have succeeded in wheedling and defrauding us out of. That was granted to Lord Selkirk, and one-tenth of it was left to the settlers. And here is a settler who, after living for years and years on his land has it taken from him, and I suppose it is now laid out in town lots and is sold at $30, $40 or $50 a foot. 1 think the government might do something for the descendants of John Cooper. If not, at least the whole story o:f the way he has been wronged and his descendants neglected will De recorded in ' Hansard.'

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE IMPERIAL CONFERENCE.
speechtext:
I endorse very cordially the claims made by my hon. friend from Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen). On more than one occasion since I have had the honour of a seat in parliament, I have heard the story of these settlers, and I have come to the conclusion that it is almost impossible to understand why their particular case was differentiated from those of other settlers of the same period and under the same circumstances. I have never to this day heard a reason given why a distinction was made in the case of this particular class of settlers. My hon, friend from Portage la Prairie has gone fully into their case, l have a number of documents connected with the case myself and have gone into the matter at different times. The hon.

gentleman lias admirably and fully exposed the merits of their claim. What is the reason that their claim has been neglected?
I take it that the reason is that their claims must' have fallen for consideration into the hands of employees of the department who viewed the claims in the purely legal 'aspect. Of course, it could easily be established that on strictly legal grounds they had no claim upon the government. And the report being to the effect that they had no claim, the ministers in charge at the time-
I do not know what their colour was- would be glad to get rid of the claim without looking 'at the equitable side of the matter. I think that at this moment, in view of the settlements that are made in the west, the government might very well take up these claims and put these dissatisfied people upon the same basis as those around them. We are told the government has a policy, that it cannot without violating that policy take up these claims and render justice. But the policy of this government seems to be singular in the extreme, our immigration policy has led us to make the freest concessions to newcomers. That we should extend facilities to newcomers when they desire to settle in the. northwest is reasonable enough, but why should we be so hard towards the old settlers, the Fenian raiders, for instance excellent Canadians [DOT]who could put forth some claim to merit acquired and who would make the very best class of settlers for the northwest? Why should we treat the Doukhobors so generously when they arrived in this country and yet adopt the policy under which we make it so difficult for good settlers from the older provinces to get any advantage in going to settle in that country. Our policy it seems to me is too generous to strangers and too hard, too rigid, too much based upon purely legal considerations when we are dealing with our own people. On the contrary, with our own people we should be most openhanded and generous with the great wealth of land we have in the west.

speakeroldname: Hon. FRANK OLIVER (Minister of the Interior).
speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE IMPERIAL CONFERENCE.
speechtext:
I do not wish to traverse the very carefully prepared and very elaborate statement of my hon. friend from Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen) at any great length and would not have done so were it not for the support which he has received. But, in view of that support, and the attitude taken by those who give that support, I think it is necessary, perhaps, to say a few words on the subject. And, if I have to do so, I might as well begin at the beginning and allude to the apology which my hon. friend from Portage la Prairie offered at the beginning of his remarks, when he said he would not be accused of obstruction in bringing up this question. I would not
have accused him of obstruction. But my hon. friend knows that ' to excuse is to accuse.' When he proffers an excuse he leaves an opening for an accusation; and it may not be out of place for us to consider just how far such an excuse was necessary in this case.
We have here a matter which was disposed of thirty-five years ago by the parliament of Canada,-disposed of finally by that parliament on a second attempt to dispose of it. That is to say, parliament dealt with the question in 1872 and. again in 1874, and it has not dealt with it since. It seems to me that a question such as this might very well have stood for a little while longer under all the special circumstances of the case, without seriously damaging it.
I notice on the Order Paper that this parliament has a great deal of business to do, pressing and important business, business which is not thirty-five years old,, and has not been off the books for that length of time, but business that is on the books and awaiting action and for which the country is demanding action, or at any rate requiring it. May I just draw the attention of the House for a few moments to some of these matters which, at the instance of my hon. friend, have been compelled to give way in order that the claims of these old settlers should be brought before parliament on this particular occasion. First, we have the motion to go into Committee of Ways and Means, to discuss, and to carry, if possible, a measure of tariff reduction which, I submit on the statement of our friends on the other side, has not been equalled in importance by any matter that has come before parliament since confederation. Surely, that was a matter that was entitled to precedence even over the claims of the old settlers, these claims of thirty-five years ago. But, even if we had disposed of that question, there are a number of other matters to which I think it might be well to draw attention. I notice, for instance, that there is a large body of legislation by orders in council dealing with the administration of the lands, timber and minerals of this country under the control of the Dominion of Canada which requires confirmation by parliament.
If it should happen that it does not receive that confirmation during this session of parliament, then this legislation by order in council becomes invalid under the statute. Surely this is a matter of somewhat pressing importance, and might well have had precedence after we had disposed of reciprocity. There is another matter I find here-speaking of matters that particularly concern my own department, and my duties in the House. There is the Manitoba Grain Act, which was brought down from the Senate after having occupied the attention of that body for a number of weeks; it is an Act that is ab-

solutely urgent, if the views and requirements of the people of the west are to be met. This Bill was brought before the House immediately before adjournment, it was not possible to get the Bill passed at that time, but it awaits consideration by this House now, it pressingly awaits consideration, otherwise it cannot be brought into effect so as to be of any advantage for the crop of this year. There is a Bill regarding Chinese immigration. We have had a debate on Chinese immigration in this House; it is known that the Chinese Act requires amendment. The Bill was brought in some time ago, it did not receive consideration then, it claims consideration now, but it cannot get it; it has to take second place to the claims made by our friends on behalf of the old settlers of the Red river. There is an important Bill respecting banks and banking under the name of the Minister of Einance on the importance of which I need not enlarge.
At six o'clock, House took recess.
* After Recess.
House resumed at eight o'clock.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE IMPERIAL CONFERENCE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the House rose at six o'clock I was mentioning a number of measures of importance before the House which might have claimed attention in preference to the subject which is now under discussion without in any degree minimizing the importance of that subject. I mentioned among other things the Bank Act which is on the Order Paper for amendment. I had not reached a conclusion in regard to that. The Bank Act was so urgent that in view of the fact that it. had not been possible to push it forward an interim Act had to be passed, and at the present time the country has failed to get the advantage of the Bank Act as prepared and made ready for the House. Another subject which is of some importance to some part of the Dominion which I might mention is an Act relating to waters in the railway belt and Peace river block of land, a matter upon the early adjustment of which depends the value of many thousands of dollars worth of property in British Columbia. A Bill of the same nature was introduced last session, it stood over, it was introduced again this session, and to-day these rights are being sacrificed for the lack of this or similar legislation. Another matter that I might mention is an amendment to the Railway Act which was under consideration in the last few days before adjournment, an amendment brought in by my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) for the purpose of protecting the rights of owners of live stock which stock has been injured by the rail-Mr. OLIVEB
way. It was not possible under the circumstances to secure the concurrence of the House in that provision at the time. It awaits the action of the House and if I understand the situation the farming interests of the west certainly demand its passage at this session. I would not use the word ' obstruction ' to characterize the very carefully prepared and well presented case laid before the House by the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr Meig-hen) in regard to these old settlers' rights, but I will say that with a question of such paramount importance as reciprocity before the House, unless the English language has lost its meaning, an amendment moved to the motion to take up that question must certainly be an obstruction of the discussion of the question, and therefore of the business of the House. I am sure that the ordinary elector will wonder how it is that, when there is this important question to be decided, and when there are these important matters upon the Order Paper which ought to receive the attention of the House, the House has plenty of time to spend in discussing the question of a right, which, to put it most mildly. is thirty-five years old, and which was decided upon by the House of Commons, and the government thirty-five years ago. Every thing in its place, there is a time during the session when matters of lesser, importance, and which are less pressing may be fairly and reasonably discussed, but I do submit that a claim of this character brought forward at this stage of the session, with the Order Paper crowded as it is, and with a discussion such as that now 'before the House going on, can scarcely m fairness be called a subject of fair or proper consideration. But, however, whatever may have been the purpose of the non. gentleman who made the motion, there is no question as to the purpose of those who support him. It was not more to secure certain so-called rights of people who are spoken of as the pioneers of Rupert's Land as to create sympathy for them in regard to the deprivation of these rights and therefore to secure disapproval of the government and its policy to a very much farther reaching extent. As to the merits of the question, I think the hon. member for Portage la Prairie stated the case very clearly and fairly when he said that the statute of limitations or the law of limitations was a right and proper law and must necessarily apply. The reason for that law is that as time goes on new conditions arise under which conditions it becomes impossible to give countenance to a certain claim because of other rights _ which have arisen under this new condition. In regard to the claim made by those pioneers, whatever may have been the merit of their claim in the first

place, and they pressed it at that time, and it was decided upon by the government and parliament of that day and decided against them, there is no question that the concession of their request to-day would not be in the best interests of western Canada or of the people of western Canada, speaking at large. There is also a difference between the granting of a claim at that day and the granting of the same claim to-day. At that time the scrip right to 160 acres had a very minimum value. It might have been worth $160, and it might not have been worth nearly so much. I doubt very much if it would be worth that much. To-day a similar scrip claim upon 160 acres would probably be worth from $1,200 to $1,600. There is a difference of ten times the value between a grant made in those days and a grant as it would be made to-day. That is an important change in the conditions which no government could fail to recognize.
On this question of the issue of scrip, the conclusion has been reached by the government that there should not be any further issue of land scrip in the western provinces. It is recognized that the issue of land scrip in the past has not resulted in the well-being of those provinces, it has not resulted to the good of the people of the provinces, it has not promoted their settlement or welfare.
In the first place when scrip was issued it was intended to act as an inducement to settlement. A man was given a property right and on the strength of that he was expected some day to occupy the land and in that way add* to the wealth and improvement of the country. But, as a matter of fact, in practice these scrip rights have been used for speculative rather than for settlement purposes in the proportion of probably five to one, and on behalf of the actual settler of the country, the man who goes in there as a homesteader to earn his right to his land, to whom the occupation of the surrounding land is of prime and vital importance, it is not advisable that there should be further issues of land scrip. If there is to be sympathy for any one it should be for the honest settler who is honestly and fairly endeavouring to establish himself on the prairie or in the woods, and who is handicapped to a very great extent by these issues of scrip which allow land to be held without occupation as halfbreed or old settlers scrip does allow it to be held, I think it would be certainly an offence lagainst the welfare 'and well (being of the country if the government should, under any possible circumstances except the fulfilment of obligations already entered into, further issue this sort of scrip. The contention that the government occupies the position of a trustee towards these people
is not well founded. In order that there shall be a trusteeship there must be a right and the hon. gentleman admitted in the very beginning of his argument that there was no right, that whatever grant was given to the old settlers who came in from 1813 to 1835 was given as an act of grace, and not as a matter of right. Then if there is no right on their part there can be no trusteeship on ours and, their claim to this grant must rest on other grounds than that; as to what grounds they can rest their claims upon I am not here to say.
It is argued that because a certain grant was made to the settlers who came in between 1813 and 1835, therefore settlers who came after 1835 are entitled to a grant. I am unable to follow the reasoning. It may be that the grant to settlers between 1813 and 1835 may have been made without due warrant for aught I know. At any rate the fact that the parliament which made that grant refused to make a grant for the time following 1835 is surely sufficient reason for this parliament to say that the case is closed, that unless a good reason can be shown, unless some tangible ground can be shown wherein these people have a tangible right, this government or this parliament should not reopen the question. So far from the fact that the government of that day did not extend the right beyond 1835 being a reason for our extending it, I submit in all fairness and all reason that the fact that they, with all the knowledge they had of all the circumstances and of their responsibility did not extend it beyond that time, is certainly not a reason why we should, unless some tangible and definite reason is produced, such as has not yet been produced.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE IMPERIAL CONFERENCE.
speechtext:
The minister treated the House to a number of reasons why nothing should be done at the present time. He says that the fact that parliament granted land to the settlers between 1813 and 1835, was no reason why the settlers coming in subsequently to that were entitled to any consideration. That might or might not be the case, but the fact that they granted land to settlers who came in between 1813 and 1835 when the conditions were much the same as the conditions after 1835, would seem to indicate that those who came in after 1835 were entitled to the same consideration. The minister has not given the House to understand that settlers who came in after 1835 came in under any more favourable circumstances than those who came in between 1813 and 1835. He says that because land is more valuable today scrip will be worth ten times as much as it was 30 years ago, and that that is a reason why we should not give a. land grant. If the consideration would be too high parliament could reduce it to a reasonable and proper amount. The

minister said that because this was a case 35 years old, it should not be settled. By the same line of reasoning the claims of the provinces for increased subsidies which have been twice granted in 40 years, should not have been granted.
The minister has criticised the opposition because we have not dealt with several Bills of great importance which might, have been passed if the opposition had not wasted so much time over the reciprocity resolutions. If the government were so ' anxious to pass these Bills they should have brought them in and attempted to pass them. The opposition have never attempted to prevent the Bills passing.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE IMPERIAL CONFERENCE.
speechtext: The opposition certainly prevented the Grain Bill and the clauses of the Railway Act relating to the killing of cattle from passing.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE IMPERIAL CONFERENCE.
speechtext: The opposition only endeavoured to secure features that would have made these fair Bills. They did not try to prevent the Bills going through. He mentioned also the Chinese Immigration Bill.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE IMPERIAL CONFERENCE.
speechtext: I, myself, presented that Bill to the House, and at the request of the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Taylor) it was allowed to stand.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE IMPERIAL CONFERENCE.
speechtext:
Why? Because of the absence of information that had been brought out by a Royal Commission and which the government would not present to the House although it had been in their possession for weeks. '
Only the other day we had to hold up the House to get that information which should have been presented before we separated on the 19th of May. Then there was the Act respecting copyrights. That was held up by the government, not by the opposition. We did not try to prevent it passing, but endeavoured to help the government to make it as useful a measure as possible. The Bill respecting banks and banking, a very important Bill, the opposition never prevented passing. We were willing to go on and discuss it, but it was held up by the government. They held it up for the whole of last session, and it was at the request of the Minister of Finance that the Bank Act was then extended for another year, to enable the government to get certain information which they thought desirable. Practically the same thing happened this year. So that in no sense can the opposition be held responsible for that Act not passing. Another Bill is an Act relating to the water in the railway belt and Peace River'block of land. Surely the hon. minister cannot say that the opposition is responsible for that Bill not passing, for the government did not bring it on or Mr. SPROULE.
attempt to pass it. Had they done so, the opposition would certainly have made no effort to prevent it passing at the earliest possible date. Then, there is the Bill to amend the Dominion Lands Act. Does the Minister of the Interior pretend to say that the opposition tried to hold that up? I heard nothing of it. So it is with a number of these Bills that he claims might have been passed but for the action of the opposition. In what way the action of the opposition prevented the government bringing on these measures and attempting to pass them I am at a loss to understand. I think that when the hon. minister thinks seriously over this again, he will feel that he did the opposition a great injustice when he tried to saddle upon them the responsibility of these Bills not passing, which they were ready to help the government to pass if the government had brought them on.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE IMPERIAL CONFERENCE.
speechtext:
The hon. the Minister of the Interior, by the statement he made in answer to the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule), has given me the text for a speech, and consequently has enabled me to contribute a little towards the obstruction of the opposition to the passing of this reciprocity matter. My speech, however, the first since the re-assembling of the House, will be a short one. The Minister of the Interior tells us thai the opposition obstructed the passing of the Grain Bill. We have the pleasure occasionally of a visit in Manitoba from the hon. minister on his passage to and fro between here and the foothills of the Rocky Mountains. On those occasions he sometimes undertakes to preach a seTmon. On a missionary tour through Manitoba a few weeks ago he preached the gospel of reciprocity. He did not discuss the Grain Bill in the city of Winnipeg, but he did so away in the northwestern part of the province, where no grain men live, and in Dominion city, in the southwestern part of the province, where no grain men live; and I will quote the words put into his mouth by two Winnipeg papers, the ' Tribune ' and the ' Free Press,' and I will characterize this statement, taken from one of these newspapers-I do not refer to it as a part of his speech, because that would he unparliamentary-as one of the meanest representations ever made on a public platform. It contains just enough fact to make it stick, but it is an untruthful representation all the same. Here is the statement:
Turning to the terminal elevator question, Mr. Oliver stated that very powerful interests were opposed to government ownership, and the solution of a commission had been decided upon by the government as an experiment. When the Bill came to the House from the Senate, where it had been discussed at length, he had asked the House to pass it without amendment, but Alexander Haggart, of Win-

mpeg, and other western members, had refused his request, and had held up the Bill. Thus the chance of having the Bill in operation for this yearns crop had been jeopardized. The west should deal with those members.
Now, let us see what was done. Important Bills of this nature are usually brought into the Commons first, and then go to the Senate; but for some unaccountable reason, the promoters of this Bill brought it into the Senate in the early part of the session, before the reciprocity resolutions were introduced into this House. There that Bill slumbered all winter, and into the early months of spring. The first opportunity we had of making any observations on that Bill was when the hon. gentleman moved the second reading; and when was that? On the last day before adjournment. It was a Bill of 242 sections. Why, it would have taken the whole of that sitting for the clerk to have read the Bill. I had the temerity to make a few observations on that Bill. Remember, it was introduced into this parliament before there was any thought of reciprocity. It makes changes in the old conditions that were asked for by the farmers, and not one section of it was objected to by the grain men. Here we have a Bill regulating the trade of one of the largest businesses in this country, in which millions of dollars are invested every year, which taxes the ability of our financial institutions to buy and store the grain and market it in foreign countries. In conversation with grain men in Winnipeg, every one of whom forgets every night more than the Minister of the Interior ever knew about the grain business, although they did not object to a clause in the Bill under existing conditions they said that it would make matters perfectly ridiculous. It would result in this, that the grain men, the merchants, and the institutions financing all that business would be sent to do business in Minneapolis, Duluth and Chicago, where they would not be subject to the discipline that is provided for in that Bill. I had the temerity to say a few words. I did not speak more than a few minutes. There were other gentlemen in this House who represented just as good a sentiment in that northwest country as the hon. Minister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver) and who had the temerity to make some observations in reference to the Bill. That whole debate did not last more than an hour, and there was not an unnecessary word said. Then what happened? The hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) rose in his place and said:

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE IMPERIAL CONFERENCE.
speechtext:
It is quite evident that this Bill can hardly be classed among the noncontentious measures; and as hours and even minutes are beginning to become very precious if we are to carry out our intention of
adjourning, I would suggest that the debate should be adjourned and the Bill stand over.
Mr. KING moved the adjournment of the debate.
So much for this Bill, and I have no doubt that a great deal I have said is applicable to the other Bills which the hon. gentleman has cited as not having passed through this House. This claim of the old settlers is thirty-five years old. Has it lost any merits? Is it barred by the Statute of Limitations? Not at all. No Statute of Limitations runs against the King, whose representative the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver) is. It would be a poor law that would not work both ways, and it would be no credit to the government if they asked for the protection of a statute which would not be any defence to them. The fact that this Bill is 35 years old does not detract in any way from its merits. I admit that these people have no legal claim, any more than the men. who fought in South Africa, or the men who received these land grants in our Northwestern country. It is >a matter of grace. However, their claim is as good to-day as it was when they first acquired it-I mean as a matter of merit.
We will continue to receive in good nature the lectures which have been given to us from time to time by the hon. gentlemen, but we shall continue to perform our duty and express our approval or disapproval of what may come from the other side of the House.

speakerposition: subtopic
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE IMPERIAL CONFERENCE.
WAYS AND MEANS-THE IMPERIAL CONFERENCE.
speechtext:
Before you leave the Chair, Mr. Speaker, I desire to refer briefly to a matter which was mentioned in this House on Friday, 21st inst., in connection with the lists in the organized or unorganized portions of Ontario. I would draw the attention of the House to the statements made by the hon. Minister of Justice with reference to the position of things. By reference to ' Hansard ' you will find that I drew the attention of the government to the position of the law with regard to the making of the lists in the unorganized districts of Ontario, and asked certain specific questions. I asked:
Has there been a proclamation under the Act of 1908 prescribing an earlier day for the making up of the voters' lists? if so, when will the work of enumeration be started and how long is it expected, from the most recent advice the government has, that it will take; and, will the government see to it that the Board of Registration is prevented in this instance from arrogating to itself the functions of government by abridging the time which by this Act is directed to be followed as far as possible.

To this the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Aylesworth) replied:
In regard to the present situation, fortunately we are not in the same position that existed three years ago No one, I presume, has any expectation that the general elections which follow upon a dissolution of this House, are any where in sight, or are at all liable to take place until there has been at least one session or perhaps two sessions more. In these circumstances there seems no danger to be apprehended that it may be found necessary an the part of the learned judges who are at present engaged in the preparation of these lists to curtail at all the time which the statute provides for taking the various steps.
I had pointed out to the Minister of Justice the very grave injustice which had been done to this country prior to the last general election by the Board of Registration being permitted to shorten the statutory periods fixed for the making up of these voters' lists, and I drew the attention of the Minister of Justice to the facts concerning the violations of the law in 1908 so that there might be no repetition of these violations at this election. I pointed out to the hon. gentleman, that the populated area in these unorganized territories of New Ontario, and for which voters' lists would be made up had been considerably enlarged since the last election, and that the means of communication were considerably more difficult than they were in 1808, therefore we were at more inconvenience than in 1908, and, if the inconvenience of shortening the time was great in 1908, it is greater still now, with the larger area and more difficult communication.
Under the machinery which governs the Dominion Elections Act, section 9a provides that the first step is a proclamation. This proclamation has to run for 30 days. After this we have the posting of the lists and then a further period of 15 days for appeal. These are all fair and reasonable periods, having regard to the immense expanse of territory to be covered and the amount of information to be obtained in order to get a fair list. In 1908, the statutory period from the 1st August to the 15th October was not sufficient to enable the preparation of the lists. As I pointed out to the House the other day, it took practically from the 1st August to midday October 26-the day of the election-to get these lists completed, and on the ground ready for the polls. As a matter of fact, by the opening of the Printing Bureau on Sunday, the running of a special train from Ottawa to Sault Ste. Marie at the expense or the government and a further train along the Algoma Central from Sault Ste. Marie to mile 68, also at the expense of the government, the lists were at the polls, completed and revised, three hours after Mr. BOYCE.
the polls had opened. That ought to be sufficient to show that the statutory periods were short enough, and that there was little to be gained along the line of doing justice to the people by shortening the time any further.
Now the hon. Minister of Justice gave a very peculiar reply, as will be seen. He said:
In these circumstances there seems no danger to be apprehended that it may be found necessary on the part of the learned judges who are at present engaged in the preparation of these lists to curtail at all the time which the statute provides for taking the various steps.
According to the information which I hold in my hand, and which was within the knowledge of the Minister of Justice, that was an attempt to deceive this House. For, at that time, the Minister of Justice knew perfectly well that, prepared in his office and signed by his deputy was a proclamation by which the time under the statute for making up these lists had been shortened to two months. Instead of allowing from the 1st of August to the 15th of October, this proclamation directed that the lists should be prepared between the 18th of July and the 18th of September. This document which was known to the minister, is in direct contradiction of the statement he made on the 21st of July. I say that such a condition of things calls for protest and strong expression of resentment which I now desire to give. One does expect, when he asks in a reasonable manner for information from a minister of the Crown, especial-ally on a mon-jpolitical subject, ox one that is supposed to be non-political, and more especially when the person of whom the question is asked is the chief judicial executive of the Dominion, that he will receive a fair statement of the facts as known to the minister. But when the minister deliberately descends to giving to the House information entirely contrary to what he knows to be correct, that calls, as I say, for a strong expression of resentment from members on both sides of the House. I ask the attention of the House to this matter, that my resentment of the minister's answer may be made known, and that the country may take knowledge of the lamentable and pitiable position to which ministers of the Crown descend to delude members on this side with inaccurate information. I hope the Minister of Justice will rise in his place now and give to the House some reasonable explanation of the extraordinary statements contained in his answer in contrast with this proclamation.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE IMPERIAL CONFERENCE.
speechtext:
I do not feel that I am called

upon to make any explanation of the matter. I am quite sure that every member of this House understood the remarks I made on Friday last in reference to the probability of an election within a short time in the future in exactly the sense in which I intended them to be understood. I am quite sure there was no one in this House who was deceived in any way by what I said, nor did I intend that anybody should be. And, especially with regard to the proclamation with reference to the preparations of the voters' lists in the unorganized portions of the province of Ontario, the hon. gentleman must attribute to his fellow members in this House a degree of lack of perception beyond the ordinary if he supposes that anyone could think another would be deceived on a subject of that sort by what was said on Friday last with a proclamation on the subject appearing on Saturday. At the time I was speaking, on Friday, I was, of [DOT]course, perfectly aware of the fact that a proclamation was pending, that the proclamation had been prepared, and would appear in the ' Gazette ' of the following day. What that has to do with what I said upon the Friday I am not able to understand. With regard to the whole question of the preparation of the voters' lists _ in the unorganized territory I have nothing to add to or subtract from what I said on Friday. I am not here defendr ing the statute referred to; that statute is not at present under consideration. When it was before a previous parliament for consideration I defended it:	I thought it
was proper legislation; I stated so then; I think_ so still; I state so still. It is an Act which is not now under the consideration of this House, the provisions of which need not be, so far as I can see, debated; at all events, it is not my intention to debate them. Under the statute, this parliament delegated to the judges of the district courts of that territory the duty of preparing the lists, having regard, as far as possible to the dates for the various steps prescribed by the provincial statute. Upon the judges that duty and responsibility rests, and that duty and responsibility is not being interferred with in any degree by the Minister of Justice, or, so far as I am aware, by any member of the government.

speechtext:
Last Friday when we adjourned the debate, it was my misfortune to have the floor. And resuming that debate this evening, I do not expect to detain the House at any great length. However, the attitude of the government and its supporters leads one on this side of the House to the necessity of taking up a longer time than would be necessary had we not a lot of gentlemen on the opposite side who are not only bound but gagged and not able to take part in this debate. We might possibly shorten our remarks in this discussion had we enlightment from gentlemen who now sit opposite us as dumb as oysters.
There are some provinces of this Dominion from 'which no one has been heard, sitting on the government side of the Douse. But on this side, every province has been heard from, except Prince Edward Island, 'and the hon. member representing that island on the opposition side will be heard from in due time. On Friday last the Minister of Finance and myself had a little discussion over the lumber question, and I endeavoured to show that the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Customs did not know their business when they were dickering at Washington on the lumber question, I was endeavouring to show that these two gentlemen, these two wandering, weary Willies, wandered away to Washington with the idea in their noddles that they understood every phase of every question in regard to every industry of this country affected by this pact, but we find that they were very remiss in regard to the lumber interest. We have heard a great deal in this House about its importance. We have heard of its importance in British Columbia the other day, and last night we heard of its importance from the Minister of Public Works who represents a constituency in New Brunswick. Now the Minister of Public Works last night, I thought, was endeavouring to come to the rescue of his friend the Minister of Finance, and was endeavouring to enlighten the House ion the shingle question. He laid great stress



on the fact that they had put the duty back to the old rate, from 50 to 30 cents a thousand on shingles. But that was not at all the argument this side was putting up-Here are two gentlemen invited down to "Washington to make a bargain with regard to reciprocity, and the lumber question comes up, the lumber industries of the two countries-. Now, my point is that, having been invited down to Washington to make this treaty, if they had had the interest of this country at heart, or the interest of the lumber industry at heart, they would have seen to it that Canadian shingles entered the United States on the same footing as United States shingles come into Canada. That would have been something like a reciprocity treaty. I endeavoured last Friday night to enlighten the Minister of Finance on this question, but the Minister of Public Works-, in coming to the rescue of his colleague in regard to shingles, carefully avoided the question of the entry of lumber into this country, partly dressed, and in some cases fully dressed. He forgot to tell us that while the Americans are allowed to send their dressed lumber or partly dressed lumber into Canada free of duty, we are not allowed to send a single board into that country if there is one scratch of a plane upon it. I want to emphasize that. I say that if the hon. gentlemen who went to Washington to make this treaty had had the interest of the country at heart, they would have seen to it that the American duty, instead of being reduced from $1.75 to $1.25, was taken off altogether.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS - RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH THE UNITED STATES.
WAYS AND MEANS - RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman is not going to be allowed to give away the trade and commerce of this country into the hands of the United States. I say he was remiss in his duty towards Canada when dealing with them in any shape or form, that he did not secure the free entry of Canadian lumber into that country the same as we give to their lumber. The hon. gentleman says that he was giving them nothing. I do not know why he should have been so anxious to deal with them at all. The Americans do not dicker with anybody unless they see some profit in it. They got everything they asked for from Canada, and if they had asked for more they would have got it. When I was speaking on Friday night I referred to the danger of this country dealing with the Americans in this matter at all, and in the way proposed. I was trying to show the House, as the hon. member for Vancouver says, in my weak and squeaky voice, that there was a real danger in this country entering into this pact with the United States at all. Yesterday tne Minister of Finance, when he was trying to make a little campaign speech, made light of some of the statements made by the senators and representatives on the American side. I can hardly understand why the minister should make light of those gentlemen, in face of some of the remarks they have made. This House has heard quoted over and over again the re-marks of Mr. Champ Clarke, of Mr. Wilson, the Secretary of Agriculture, of Senator McColl, of Senator Cummins, of Iowa, of Mr. Prince, of Illinois.
I am not going to trouble you with them all, but I have one or two that I wish to bring to the attention of the House. Mr. Prince, of Illinois, in the House of Representatives some time ago, made this statement:
What is the history of the American people?
I want to lay this before the hon. gentlemen who have British blood coursing through their veins, and to ask them whether they feel like entering into a pact with the United States, when- the gentlemen who represent the United States have in their breasts this sentiment, which has been expressed by them time and time again:
What is the history of the American people? We might as well be frank and honest. Americans went into Texas, Americanized it, and it was annexed as part of this great Union. Americans went into Hawaii, Americanized it, and annexed it. And if these bright young men that the President speaks of in his speech- these clever, active, virile, vigorous young men from the farms of Illinois and the northern states, the thousands and hundreds of thousands of them-go up into that nortkland, 92 or 100 and more on this side, as against seven on the other, what do you think will be the effect of it ?	[DOT]

That is how they feel about it. What will the effect be once they get the upper hand in this country? They will Americanize it as they did Texas and other parts. I am not going to bother the House with any more extracts. This is a feeling that exists with nine-tenths of the American people to-day. In travelling all over this country, as I have done during the time that this subject has been up for discussion before the House, I have met a great many American people and I am safe in saying that nine-tenths of them consider that this is the first step towards being annexed to them sooner or later. I am sure there are dozens of hon. gentlemen on this side of the House, and some on the other side of the House who know that these people take that view. There is a real danger of the American people getting the upper hand in this country. There is a real danger of the American people getting the upper hand of our farming interests. We are one as against twelve. There has been much stress is laid on the fact that we are opening up a great market for our farmers, but the fact has been lost sight of that we are opening up a great market for the American farmers, a market of twelve to one for the goods that come into this country. If you are entering into negotiations with a corporation, whether you go into the deal with them or not, they stand out always for the best end of it. In this matter they have stood out and got everything they asked for. I think I would be remiss in my duty to my constituents, and to the people of Canada, and that I would also be ignoring the traditions that I was brought up to believe in, and my devotion to British institutions if I were to record my vote in behalf of this pact. I intended placing on ' Hansard ' some other matters here that are very pertinent to this question, but I will reserve them until some future time. They refer to the trade and commerce of this country. This is the second time that I have had an opportunity of placing my views before the House on this matter, and I was most anxious to have the hon. Minister of Customs (Mr. Paterson) in his place. He may be home sleeping but he is not attending to what he is paid to attend to by the people of Canada. Here is a question so important that, according to the hon. Minister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver), all other business before the House has to stand aside. If it is so important why is it not necessary for the Minister of Customs to be in the House. We have also the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir Bichard Cartwright). Where is he-asleep in the Senate chamber? When we require any information from his department we are told by the right hon. Prime Minister, or some other hon. gentleman who might be leading the House, that in the absence of the Minister of Trade 3203
and Commerce, he is not able to reply, but he will find out from the old gentleman just as soon as he can, and will bring the information to the House. The people of this country expect active gentlemen at the head of every department of this or any other government. I am not casting any reflection on any gentleman who is sitting in this House in that regard, but it is an outrage when we have an important matter such as this is before the House that we have not the Minister of Customs and the Minister of Trade and Commerce in their places. I have perhaps taken up as much time as I ought, and unless the hon. Finance Minister (Mr. Fielding) wants to tackle me on the lumber question, I do not know very well what I should say. But. just one matter comes to my mind in regard to the lumber interests as to how this measure affects the farmer. I said the other day that I would much prefer seeing a duty of $2 per thousand placed on southern pine and Michigan hemlock to seeing the duty removed from lumber entering Canada, and the Minister of Finance at that time said that it was not their policy and that they did not intend to do any such thing. But he forgot that he was throwing a stone in the face of the farmers in the newer parts of this country. The farmers of new or northern Ontario who are ocupying farms largely covered with hemlock and other cheap grades of timber heretofore have had a fairly good market, but owing to the fact that the gentlemen who own the southern timber have large tracts of land, and that their payments are now pressing them, they are making a dumping ground of Canada for their lumber. The gentlemen who own these limits in the south are only paying 50 cents per thousand feet stumpage, they are only paying a nominal yearly ground rent and they are geting their lumbering done at fifty and sixty cents per day by negro labour, as against the lumbermen and farmers of this country who receive from $2.50 to $3.75 per day. That southern lumber is being dumped into Canada as against the farmer of Ontario, at least, and I have no doubt the same condition obtains in Quebec, New Brunswick and British Columbia and is sold at much below the price at which the farmers are able to produce their hemlock and spruce timber.	\
As I said the other night, you will find every mill yard in the district which I have the honour to represent piled high with lumber that should be used by the Canadian people that is now standing rotting on the piles, while American lumber is allowed in to take its place. I hope our weak and humble efforts will have so affected the government and the gentlemen responsible for the delay and obstruction in the passage of the several measures

referred to by the Minister of the Interior, that they will at once grant an appeal to the people. The Minister of the Interior says that some very important matters have had to lie over because we chose to act in the interests of our constituents and to debate this subject, and he says we are obstructionists. I say the whole responsibility for any loss of time or of anything else that has been caused by this reciprocity debate rests on the government, because, at the beck and call of the American President, they have introduced what I might call a crime against the people of this country, this pact with the American government. If they had not introduced this measure the wheels of progress would have gone on in this House and we would have been able to pass the important measures about which the Minister of the Interior is so much concerned. The right hon. the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance understand that the wheels of progress can only go on in this House when they give way to the will of those who represent the majority of the people, I ask them to advance it and to advance it in the quickest way we know, that is by going before the people who have sent us here and asking them to tell us how we should vote on this very important question.
