speechtext:
SHARPE (North Ontario) I had hoped that the government and their supporters would have seen tit to withdraw from this unfortunate pact after having had an opportunity during the recess of consultation with their supporters and after reflection and analysis, and after having fully digested the details of this agreement. Of course I quite understand that such an attitude would have entailed heart burnings and humiliations and possibly withdrawal from the cabinet of the two ministers responsible for this unfortunate agreement. I suppose it is too much to expect such self-sacrifice from the hon. gentlemen who went to Washington to negotiate this important treaty on behalf of the farmers of this country. I would like to know where the champions of this agreement are to-day. Their voices are silent as the tomb; outside of the cabinet ministers no voices are raised in defence of this agreement, it has assumed the position of an undefended case. When the Finance Minister first introduced this agreement an hon, member supporting the government rushed from the House and telegraphed to the paper supporting the government in his constituency that it was the greatest act of diplomacy in the history of Canada, of great importance to the farmers of Ontario and showed statesmanship almost divine. After the hon. gentleman had recovered from his spasm and after the facts in regard to the twelve Mr. SMYTH.
favoured nations had been extracted from the hon. gentleman, I might almost say at the point of the bayonet, by the leader of the opposition, after the subject had been thoroughly discussed and the hostility of the people of the country aroused, the hon. gentleman to whom I refer was as dumb as an oyster, he has refused to raise his voice in the House in defence of the agreement.
One of the most remarkable features in connection with this whole treaty is the absolute lack of information on the part of our plenipotentiaries when they went to negotiate it. Our representatives going to Washington had no data or statistics or detailed information upon which they could form an intelligent judgment or negotiate an intelligent treaty for the farmers of this country. In their hurry and anxiety to complete this agreement and to accomplish something to divert attention from their long record of maladministration, of departmental inefficiency and their foolish naval policy, they neglected to fortify themselves with the necessary data which was in the possession of the American government.
On the 16th of March, I moved for a return in connection with certain important commodities which I, in my innocence, thought the ministers would have had under their hands. The return for which I moved called for the average prices of butter and eggs in London, England, for the past five years in comparison with the prices respectively in eastern provinces, in Montreal, in Toronto, in Minneapolis, in Chicago, in Detroit, in Buffalo, in Boston and in New York. The Minister of Agriculture took no exception to the order gping and said he would supply the information in the course of a few days. After many days they refused to bring down the return and this was the letter that was laid upon the table of the House.
Trade and Commerce Department, Ottawa, 25th March, 1911. Order of the House.
Sir,-I beg to return you herewith your reference No. 172 for statement showing comparative prices of butter and eggs in London, England, and certain points in Canada and the United States. This department has no information upon the subject. Such average prices of butter and eggs, however, are published in trade papers all over the world which can be referred to by any one desiring the information.
I have the honour to be, Sir,
Your obedient servant,
F. C. T. O'HARA, Deputy Minister.
Thomas Mulvey, Esq.,
Under Secretary of State,
Ottawa.
The butter and egg industries are two of the most important branches of farming

in the province of Ontario, an-d you would at least expect that the two ministers negotiating an important treaty like this would have had detailed information in regard to the comparative prices in the three countries. I also asked some questions in reference to the lack of information on the part of our representatives at Washington. The questions and answers appear in the ' Hansard ' of April 10, 1911. They are as follows:
1.	Was the purpose of entering into negotiations for reciprocity with the United States to secure better prices for Canadian produce?
The answer by the Finance Minister was:
The purpose of entering into negotiations for reciprocity with the United States was to obtain that expansion of market for Canadian products which has been sought by all governments in Canada since the formation of the Dominion.
An absolute evasion of the question which conveyed no information to any one requiring the answer to that simple question. I further asked:
2.	Were the representatives of Canada before entering upon the negotiations supplied with comprehensive data and statistics collected by experts and officials covering a considerable period and showing a comparative list of prices of all products in the principal markets of Canada and the United States?
3.	If so, will data and statistics be available to the members of the House by laying them on the table of the House?
4.	Generally speaking, how do the prices of farm products in the United States compare with the prices in Canada?
5.	Upon what information is the answer to the preceding question based?
The answer to these questions was:
2 and 5. These questions have been fully discussed in the House since the bon. member placed his question on the notice paper and the views of the government thereon have been stated.
While the question was on the Order Paper, the discussion to which the Minister of Finance referred took place on the 6th of April, and daring that discussion we had this remarkable statement by the Minister of Finance. Speaking of the commissioners appointed by the United States government to thoroughly investigate conditions in Canada, he said:
That commission has been conducting investigations not only here but in other countries, and the information was probably necessary for onr American neighbours, when they were entering upon a new and radical departure from their past fiscal policy.
As though we were not entering on as radical a change in our fiscal policy as the ministers were in theirs. He further goes on:
No such tariff commission and no such information was required to enable this government to deal with the question of reciprocity in natural products. There was no need of statistics to satisfy this government that reciprocity in natural products was a good thing.
That is a most remarkable admission on the part of the Minister of Finance. He admits categorically that they had no information or statistics. He claims that they were possessed of sufficient knowledge in a general way that reciprocity in natural products was a good thing for Canada, and consequently, without fortifying themselves with detailed information such as was in the possession of the United States representatives, they went to Washington and negotiated this treaty. Therefore, they find that it is not meeting with the approval and endorsation of the people of Canada. The hon. Minister of Finance made this further statement:
What we have done is no departure front the policy of Canada; it is in accordance with the policy of Canada for forty years.
That was a most remarkable admission on the part of the Minister of Finance. Contrast the position of the representatives of Canada with the position of the United States government. The United States government during the previous months had a full staff of experts travelling through the United States and Canada gathering information in order to enable them to come to an intelligent decision [DOT]upon these important matters. The hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Sifton), in his discussion of this question, deals with this important phase of the matter. On page-4475 of ' Hansard ' be says:
Then, we should have had, I think, some comparative statements of prices. This whole question relates to markets and to prices. It would have been a comparatively small matter for a body of experts employed by the government to have got for us a comparative list of the prices of the principle commodities, in the United States, in Canada, and in the other countries concerned. But we have not received it.
Then I ask, in the name of all that is reasonable, how can the members of this House come to an intelligent decision on this question without the necessary data and statistics which were in the possession of the United States plenipotentiaries when this treaty was negotiated? If we look at the documents prepared by the experts of the United States government, we shall see what mountains of information they were possessed of. They did not go into this negotiation blindfolded; they went with information that had been collected for months in the United States and in Canada. I have a copy of document No. 849 regarding reciprocity with Canada, prepared by

the experts of the United States government, and containing 132 closely written pages. We could not get any information from our representatives. They refused to produce it if they had any. That information would be detrimental to their side of the case; it would show that the prices of staple farm products are higher in this country than on the American side, and that consequently the whole purpose and object of this agreement falls to the ground. Any reasonable man who looks at the matter in this light must come to the conclusion that the action of this government, in negotiating this treaty at this particular time, was both premature and unwise. It was premature, because they were anticipating the action of the Democratic party, who had won the elections for Congress on the promise that they would reduce the tariff. They were, in fact, negotiating a live treaty with a dead party. Both the Reform party in Canada and the Republican party in the United States were becoming discredited by their long terms in office, and they sought to divert public attention from their records of mal-adminis-tration. If this government had held its hand for a short time, this country would have got in a short time all the advantages, if there are any, of the treaty, without making the sacrifices therein entailed. Not only was the action of the government premature, but it was unwise, because the facts extracted from the Minister of Fin-amce, and the facts prepared by the experts of the United States government, show conclusively that the prices of staple farm products in Canada are higher than they are in the United States, and consequently the whole purpose and object of this agreement falls to the ground. It is not much wonder that this unfortunate agreement has been prematurely and unwisely entered into by our representatives, when we have signal displays of ignorance of its provisions on the-part of various ministers of the Crown. We find the Minister of Agriculture, in discussing this treaty on the 28th of March, speaking of the important commodity of potatoes as follows:
In 12 years of high duties the United States accepted from Canada $11,000,000 worth of potatoes more than they sent into Canada.
Now, the trade returns prepared by the Minister of Agriculture's own department show that during the years from 1901 to 1910 we exported to the United States less than $2,000,000 worth of potatoes, and that the total value of potatoes exported from Canada to the United States during the ten years from 1901 to 1910 was $1,958,886 worth, and that we imported from the United States into Canada $1,419,651 worth, a balance, in out favour, in the ten years Mr. SHARPE (Ontario).

Agriculture	was out	only $10,500,000.
Then we had the Minister of Inland Revenue, who is the owner and editor of the ' Daily Times,' published in Victoria, writing an editorial in that paper of the date of July 12, 1911, containing the following:
It is our duty to point ont that it is not part of the proposal nnder the reciprocity agreement to allow American-made shingles to enter Canada free.
As a matter of fact, the agreement provides for shingles to come in free.

speechtext:
The hon. minister said it is not the object of this agreement to allow American made shingles to come into Canada free-another exhibition on the part of a minister of the Crown showing that he is not familiar with the terms of the agreement. We had another exhibition of this kind from the Postmaster General, who was dilating upon the excellencies of this agreement. The hon. Postmaster General is usually well informed, particularly in regard to matters connected with his own department, but when he comes to discuss the question of Fisheries and lobsters, he is in deep water. The hon. Postmaster General was telling us what an excellent thing it would be for the fishermen of the maritime provinces to have' free access for their lobsters into the United States markets, when the hon. member for Digby (Mr. Jameson) arose and informed him that lobsters had been on the free list for a great many years.
Then we had the hon. Minister of Customs (Mr. Paterson) one of the plenipotentiaries who went to negotiate this all important treaty-a man supposed to know it from cover to cover. The hon. Minister of Customs was questioned with regard to an important commodity called talc. He

said that talc was the material from which talcum powder was made, and that talcum powder was used as a toilet preparation. But, the talc contemplated by this agreement is the talc used for the manufacture of paper, which the Americans wished to import into their country free of duty. If hon. gentleman will refer to page 6 of schedule A they will find it covers ' talc, ground, bolted or precipitated, naturally or artificially, not for toilet use.' Even the agreement did not provide for talc used for toilet purposes, being exported into United States free of duty.
When you have two ministers of the crown, supposed to be familiar with the contents of the treaty, and the industrial and commercial conditions of this country, so unfamiliar with the terms of their own agreement; how can you expect the members of this House or the public at large to pass an intelligent judgment upon the agreement, unless they are supplied with all possible data and statistics? What else can you expect when two Ministers of the Crown, one an ex-newspaper editor and the other a biscuit manufacturer, who took precious good care that the industry in which his money is invested is not to be prejudiced in any way, go to Washington, and negotiate for 5,000,000 farmers; without the assistance or advice of the representatives of the interests affected, and this is the result. It seems to me we were sending a couple of political quack doctors down to that specialist, Dr. Taft, at Washington, and that they brought back a reciprocity pill, the ingredients of which and the effect of which they were ignorant, and .are asking the Canadian people to swallow it. It reminds me of the old nursery rhyme; ' Open your mouth, shut your eyes, and we will give you something that will make you healthy, wealthy and wise.' 'But' say the Canadian people 'supposing the pill kills us?' The answer is 'Then you will be none the wiser.' 'But, supposing it almost kills us?' The answer to that is 'if perchance you survive, then you can punish us by turning us out of office.' ' But supposing by any possibility it might help us?' 'Then, we are the heaven bom statesmen, our friends describe us.*
I placed a question on the Order Paper, bnt the hon. Minister of Finance did not give me what I conld call an unequivocal answer. I desired to know the object and purpose of this agreement. The hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) ?nd other members of the Cabinet said that this agreement was for the benefit of the farmers, but the hon. Secretary of State (Mr. Murphy) said that it was for the benefit of the consumer.

Finally, Mr. Murpliy held that^ this was a poor man's agreement and that it cut down the vested interests and middlemen who were so clamorous against it.
The base of the agreement is the cheapening of the workmen's food; it is based on the elemental principle of the greatest good for. greatest numbers (cheers).
The hon. Secretary of State was going around making campaign speeches and saying that this is a poor man's agreement, on the other hand other members of the government were saying that the agreement was for the benefit of the farmer-raising the prices. In the 'Ottawa Citizen' of April 2nd, the hon. Sec-eretary of State is reported as follows;
' This was essentially a poor man's agreement,' continued the speaker. Onions, butter, cabbages, beans, milk and many other articles, staples of the workingman's domestio life, would all be cheapened. In fact, upon this the treaty was primarily based.
How can the ministry reconcile these two positions? They must either accept the one or the other Are they not fooling the country in some way or another?
On the floor of the House here we had the hon. Minister of Finance, the_ non. Minister of Customs and the hon. Minister of Agriculture all stating that the object of this treaty was for the purpose of raising the prices for the farmers-that it was a farmers' agreement. The _ Tight hon. the Prime Minister in speaking in this House on March 7, 1911, used this language :
I stated a moment ago that the_ agreement we made is simply to get better prices for the products of tbe Canadian farmer.

speechtext:
We have not hurt the manufacturers and will not do so. We have benefited the farmer and the consumer. When the time comes we will sweep the country-from the Atlantic to the Pacific.
Did you ever listen to such absolute humbug and nonsense? It promises everything to everybody. Is it not a perfect classic of contradiction? If the right hon. leader of the government can convince the manufacturers that he is not going to hurt
them, and	then if	he	can	convincethe farmer	that he	is	not	going tohurt him;	and if	he	can	convincethe consumer that	he	is	not going
to hurt him, but benefit him-if he can perform that impossible task, I should not be surprised if he could sweep the country. The farmers are to be benefited -how? By raising their prices. The consumers are to be benefited-how? By lowering their prices. What kind ol mental gymnastics is required to perform a task like that? It has become definitely known by the investigation and report of the experts appointed by the United States government, who, as I have said, went throughout the cities of the United States and Canada, that the prices of staple farm products in Canada are a great deal higher than they are in the United States. On April 10, I asked the Minister of Finance the following question:-
1. Was the purpose of entering into negotiations for reciprocity with the United States to secure better prices for Canadian produce?
And The Minister of Finance answered:-
1. The purpose of entering into negotiations for reciprocity with the United States was to obtain that expansion of market for Canadian products which has been sought by all governments in Canada since the formation of the Dominion.
The hon. gentleman speaks of the expansion of markets for ouir products. A glorious expansion to get into a market where they are exporting the same produce that we have to sell! a glorious expansion to get into a market where the prices, are lower than our own! A glorious expansion when this is obtained at the expense of throwing open our markets not only to the ninety or one hundred millions in the United States, hut to the three or four hundred millions that make up the favoured nations.
Now, personally, I am unalterably opposed to reciprocity, upon a great many grounds. Some of these grounds have been mentioned by others, but I make no apology for repeating them. I do not expect that any expression of opinion that I give in this House will change hon. members on your right, Mr. Chairman. But I do expect that my views will he conveyed to my constituents, and they will see

upon what grounds I am opposing this * agreement. I think this is a most unfortunate junction in our affairs for the entering into a reciprocity agreement. As every .person admits, Canada has been enjoying an era of great prosperity, and we should be content to allow ourselves to work out our own destiny without interference from or subjection to the United States. Hon. Sir George W. Ross, who occupied a prominent position in the ranks of the Reform party for many years, and who was premier of the province of Ontario, has spoken in no uncertain tone against reciprocity. He gave an illustration to the people of Canada of their position. He spoke about an aged man who, though in good health, wanted to get better. And his epitaph was:-
I was well; I wanted to he better; and here I lie.
_ There has been no demand or sentiment in Canada for reciprocity. In fact, the Minister of Militia (Sir Frederick Borden) in an interview in Boston on the 28th of October last, while these negotiations were in progress, stated, as reported in the Montreal ' Herald ' that ' the attitude of the people of Canada was to let well enough alone.' That should be the attitude of the government which is boasting of its surpluses, and of the prosperity of Canada, which .they claim are due to their ability in administering the affairs of the country, but which we claim arise in spite of their efforts, and in spite of the effect of their administration.
Another reason why I am opposed to reciprocity is the fact that if we are not ingrates, if we have any gratitude at'all, if we have any commercial favours to give, we ought to give them to our own kith and kin, who are furnishing us with the money to develop our natural resources. It was British, and not United States, capital that developed Canada. It was British capital that constructed the Grand Trunk railway, that constructed the Canadian Pacific railway, that constructed the Grand Trunk Pacific, that constructed the Intercolonial. It was British capital that constructed our great canal systems, the Welland, the Soo, the Cornwall, and the Rideau canals. We borrowed millions from Great Britain to build extensions to these lines. We are looking to the British market to-day to build our Hudson Bay railway, the Georgian Bay canal, and a new Welland canal. British capital built our cities, paved our streets, organized our banks, supplied us with capital for our commercial and industrial enterprises. Then if we have any favours to offer we should offer them to Great Britain, and not to the United States.
Another reason why I am opposed to this reciprocity pact is the fact that in days gone by, when Canada was in a position that she required the markets of the United States, our overtures were rejected. Time after time when our representatives went to Washington seeking access to their markets, they slammed the door in our faces. Consequently now, when we have climbed the long hill of prosperity, when we are not in need of their markets, when we are independent of their markets, there is no reason why we should make sacrifices in order to gain access to those markets which we no longer require. This country, and especially the older portions of this country, have been settled by the United Empire Loyalists, men who were driven out of the United States in 1776, dispossessed of their property, whose wives and children were subjected to the rigours of a northern clime on account of their loyalty to the British Empire. Since that historic occasion the United States has time after time endeavoured to gain control of this country, but we have always swept back the Americanizing influences. We find in the constitutioif of the United States in 1776, incorporated in one of the articles, a standing invitation to the provinces of Canada to join the American union. But upon that occasion we swept back the American influences. In 1812 when Great Britain was engaged in a life and death struggle with the dictator of the world, the United States attempted to take advantage of her necessities, and we had the war of 1812. And again we swept back the Americanizing influences on that occasion. In 1866 the United States denounced reciprocity in order to starve Canada into annexation or submission. But the result was that instead of being starved into submission, with Canadian pluck, and energy, and enterprise, we built up the Canadian confederation, and again we swept back the Americanizing influences. In 1866 and 1870 we had the Fenian raids, which were fostered and abetted in United States territory, and again Canadians swept back the Americanizing influence. In 1891 we had the Reform party under the leadership of the present Prime Minister, again pandering to Americanizing influences, and introducing a policy which 'they called unrestricted reciprocity, a policy which was instrumental in driving a great many noted men from the Reform ranks, just as the policy of 1911 is driving many noted men from their ranks to-day. We had the greatest intellect that the Reform party possessed upon that occasion, the Hon. Edward Blake, denouncing the policy of unrestricted reciprocity of 1891, and forsaking the party on account of the Americanizing tendencies of that policy. Again the people responded nobly when they were asked, and they swept back the Americaniz-

mg influences. Now in 1911 we have our old friend reappearing in another guise. The unrestricted reciprocity of 1891 will ultimately come from the present agree-tnent if it is carried into effect. The farmers of this country are not going to see their protection swept away, and allow the manufacturers to be in full possession of their protection. If the protection that is now accorded to the farmers is swept away, they will insist upon equal treatment being meted out to the manufacturers. Consequently the policy that is proposed to-day in this reciprocity pact if carried into effect will inevitably lead to unrestricted reciprocity, and we think to absorption and annexation to the United States. This present agreement is the skeleton of 1891. It reminds me of a story I heard of two small boys playing in the house of one of the boy's father who was a doctor. One of them was rummaging about the house and came to a closet where there was a skeleton. He asked the doctor's son what that was. Oh, he says, it is my father's first patient. This reciprocity pact is Doctor Laurier's first patient. We killed it in 1891, and I anf satisfied that it will remain a skeleton after the election of 1911. We have, as I say, on all these numerous occasions swept back the Americanizing tendencies that have cropped up from time to time, and when the elections of 1911 are over I am satisfied the Canadian people will again demonstrate their loyalty to the mother of nations.
We have heard a great deal about the national effect of this agreement, what its ultimate effect will be on the future of Canada; and we have been taken to task some times very severely by hon. members to the right of the Speaker, notably by the Minister of Public Works only last night, ridiculing the suggestion that this agreement would ultimately result in Canada coming under the control of the United States. I want to show that these dangerous tendencies towards annexation with the United States have not been pointed out only by Conservatives, tout that prominent Liberals all over this country,_ from one end to the other, have signalized the danger to our national institutions if this agreement is carried into effect. We had the Board of Trade of the city of Toronto, a representative body of men, condemning this agreement by 298 votes to 13. Mr. Gour-lay, the president of the Board of Trade, voted in support of the resolution, and Sir Edmund Walker, who is a prominent Liberal, used this language:
For many years he had been in business in Canada and in the United States, and the people of.the latter country he knew well. It was in the true interest of Canada, Sir Edmund said, for her to remain in the British connection, without interest or contact from the Mr. SHABPE (Ontario).
south. We should develop our own nation in our own way, and his experience had deepened . the conviction that we should not become American.
Then we have the resolution of the associated Boards of Trade of the whole' prov-vince of Ontario, by a vote of 97 to 18 condemning in the strongest language this reciprocity agreement. One of the preambles of that resolution was in this language :
And whereas the proposed agreement would weaken the ties which bind Canada to the empire, and to avoid the disruption of trade referred to, Canada would be forced to closer relations with the United States, which would still further weaken those ties, and make it more difficult to avert political union with the United States.
Be it, therefore, resolved, that in the opinion of this convention of the Ontario Associated Boards of Trade the proposed agreement threatens Canadian nationality and autonomy, and is opposed to the true interests and should not be ratified.
Mr. Gourlay, President of the Board of Trade and a very prominent Liberal, speaking upon that resolution, is reported to the Toronto press to have used the following language:	.

Because the present unexampled prosperity of Canada is the result of the policy which has been pursued in the development of her trade and of her natural resources. Because it is essential to the continued national unity and development of Canada that no trade relations with any country should be agreed to by Canada on any basis which would check the growth and development _ of trade between the various parts of Canada with each other, or between Canada and the various parts of the empire; and because the proposed reciprocity agreement between Canada and the United States of America would seriously check the growth and development of this trade.
8. Because the agreement as proposed would weaken the ties which bind Canada to_ the empire, and because the unrestricted reciprocity which would naturally follow would still ' further weaken those ties and make it more difficult to avert political union with the United States.

Surely the language contained in that resolution could not be stronger, and surely the government ought to pay some attention to language which is couched in such strong terms coming from such prominent supporters as these gentlemen are. We find that all sections of the community from the Atlantic to the Pacific are opposed to this reciprocity pact. The Eev. Dr. McLeod, of
the maritime provinces, a prominent Baptist conducting a religious and not a trade paper in the interest of his esteemed denomination, the Baptist denomination, expresses his opinion very decidedly upon this question. He was ill and unable to direct his paper and during his absence an item slipped into the paper unknown to him favouring this agreement. The moment Dr. McLeod noticed this article he gave expression to his disapproval of that sentiment in the following paragraph which appeared in the next issue of the paper:
The editor, still unable to do any work whatever on the paper, having had his attention called to the article, entitled ' Reciprocity/ on page one, of March 1, feels impelled to repudiate every sentiment and shade of sentiment in it which approves of the proposed reciprocal trade arrangement now under consideration by the parliaments of Canada and the United States.
He regards the proposed reciprocity agreement as a deadly blow at the true national life of beloved Canada. He wants this statement of his strong conviction to go to his readers, lest he may never pen another sentence. This is the day of our country's peril.
'GOD SAVE CANADA!'
It is very apropos at this juncture that I should read one or two extracts from that famous manifesto that was issued to the electors of Canada by our late, esteemed leader, Sir John A. Macdonald. On the first page, I notice this sentence which is peculiarly apropos at this juncture:
Our policy in respect thereto is to-day what it has been for the past thirteen years, and is directed by a firm determination to foster and develop the varied_ resources of the Dominion by every means in our power consistent with Canada's position as an integral portion of the British Empire. To that end we have laboured in the past and we propose to continue in this work to which we have applied, ourselves of building up on this continent, under the flag of England, a great and powerful nation.
Further on he says:
It would, in my opinion, inevitably result in the annexation of this Dominion to thei United States.

The advocates of unrestricted reciprocity on this side of the line deny that it will have such an effect

Just as they are contending that this will have such an effect.
-though its friends in the United States urge as the" chief reason for its adoption that unrestricted reciprocity would he the first step in the direction of political union.
Is it not a most remarkable parallel? We have hon. members of the government and their followers stating that the present reci-

procity agreement will not have the effect that a great many reformers think it will have, namely, bring us into annexation with and absorption by the United States, while upon that occasion we had the warn-ing_ of our old chieftain that unrestricted reciprocity in 1891, would inevitably lead to annexation. The positions of the parties are similar in 1891 and 1911.

A straw shows how the wind bloyvs. We had the other day in the city of Detroit, a meeting of the most influential character of any ever held in the United States, the National Editorial Association. I suppose the members of that association have more influence in moulding public opinion and directing the affairs of the United States than those of any other association in America. The Toronto ' Star ' publishes a dispatch from Detroit which shows that the editors of the newspapers and magazines of the United States are talking nothing but annexation, they believe that this agreement will ultimately lead to the annexation of Canada to the United States. The dispatch reads:
There is much speculation among the editors as to what kind of reception they will receive during their stay in Canada. On the opening day of the convention several speeches were made in which ' Union ' with Canada was strongly advocated. So much was said along this line that a great many of the delegates have been dubbed ' annexation boosters.'
Here we have a society of editors in a regularly organized meeting on our very border discussing annexation and called ' annexation boosters ' to further the reciprocity pact not only in the United States but in Canada. The discussions were so repugnant to the feelings of Mr. Justice Sutherland, of the High Court of Ontario, formerly a respected member of this House, that he publicly rebuked them at the convention, and this is the report of what he said:
Judge Sutherland, _ of Toronto, Ont., on the floor of the convention took exception to the union sentiment and spoke warmly against it.

In the light of these expressions of opinion, in the light of the trend of the press of the United, States, can we close our eyes to the fact that the leading men and the leading newspapers of the United States are absolutely convinced that the destiny of Canada, if this agreement is adopted, will be to fly the Stars and Stripes instead of the Union Jack.
Another reason that has been advanced in this House against this pact, and it is a very valid and strong reason, is the diversion of trade that it will cause from east to west to north and -south channels-what has been called the s-ectionalization of Canada. After the denouncement of the reciprocity treaty in 1866 Canada had a difficult task to perform. Farmers were ruined and people were in distress, but there was no surrender. Canada commenced by forming a confederation in 1867, and began the slow climb up the hill of prosperity, and the people toiled and worked in order to form the country into a confederation, and a strong nationality. Sir John A. Macdonald constructed the Canadian Pacific railway in order to have a transcontinental system to' bind the provinces together. The present leader of the government inaugurated the Grand Trunk Pacific for the same purpose, and in introducing the Bill into the House, and in arguments in favour of it throughout the length -and breadth of the country, he pointed out the desirability of Canada being free and independent of the United States. He said that it was desirable that we should not be bound up with the bonding privilege, which might be withdrawn by the United States at any time, that if we wanted to be -a self-contained nation as a part of the British Empire, and independent of the United States, we must have more transportation facilities; and for that reason, and that reason alone, he asked the Canadian people for their en-dorsation of the Grand Trunk Pacific scheme. Then two Canadians, captains of finance, Mackenzie and Mann, have constructed the Canadian Northern railway. If there is one province which is vitally interested in this question, and which has been struck to the heart by this reciprocity agreement, it is the province of Ontario. It is the richest and most populous province in the Dominion of Canada. The farmers of that province have mortgaged their farms, the people have pledged their future, fox the success of these great -enterprises. They furnished the greater share' of the capitai that constructed them; and now when we are in a position to derive some advantage from them, why should we, because a few partisan Liberal grain growers in the west may possibly get a few cents more for their wheat, allow the traffic of those lines to ibe diverted to the -south, and '

I am addressing myself at the present time to the shipping interest, in which th-e province of Ontario is vitally interested. The old reciprocity treaty-, may have benefited certain interests. I am speaking of an interest that is going to be vitally injured if the present agreement goes into effect, and I am going to show that the shipping interest was vitally injured by the old reciprocity treaty. In 1854 the Canadian carrying trade on the St. Lawrence amounted to $33,633,128. The very next year. after the treaty went into effect this trade fell to $15,208,600, a decrease of over $18,000,000. In 1854 the vessels engaged in that trade numbered 1,416, rated at 618,926 tons with 20,301 sailors at Quebec. In the next year after the treaty went into effect these figures fell to 474 vessels, rated at 348,800 tons with 11,902 sailors at Quebec. In 1854 the tonnage of our sea-going vessels arriving _ and departing from fouT of the leading St. Lawrence ports amounted to 1,487,897 tons. The very next year after the treaty went into effect the tonnage fell to 870,794 tons. In 1854 the total value of the exports and imports at Montreal and Quebec was $42,000,000. The next year after the treaty went into effect they dropped to $28,000,000.
Another objection which has been raised and I think appropriately raised, against this arrangement, is its lack of permanence, the danger of entanglement with the United States, the danger of giving offence. Our trade routes have been established by successive government's from east to west. If this reciprocity pact goes into effect the trade routes will undoubtedly be changed to north and south channels. Eight millions of people have very little chance against one hundred millions of people. Uncle Sam will wield the' Big Stick, as he has wielded it before. Once let our trade routes be turned north and south, and we develop and -encourage vested interests which will fight to retain those routes, no matter how detrimental the arrangement

may be to other interests in the country. If this agreement goes into effect, and the routes are developed north and south, the United States can force other concessions from us by threatening to abolish and denounce the agreement, and throw our newly established trade relations into disorder. We have the great, free, open and independent market of Great Britain. Why should we hesitate what we should cultivate and preserve?
There are a great many constitutional and economical objections, as well as national and imperial objections, to this agreement. We are supposed to be living in a democratic age, enjoying responsible government. But, as has been said by the hon. member for Brandon, who was a member of the cabinet during the election of 1900, 1904 and 1908, there was no mention in any of those elections of this reciprocity question. He was in charge of the campaign for the Liberal party in the western provinces, and at none of those elections was this question mooted.
We are charged with inconsistency because the leaders of the Conservative party in days gone by endeavoured to secure reciprocity with the United States upon fair and equitable terms. I would ask, Mr. Speaker, if that is a reasonable argument? We had the right hon. the leader of the government, the hon. the Minister of Finance, the hon. the Minister of Public Works, and the hon. Minister of Customs reading extracts from speeches made in bygone days, showing that the Conservative party in these days were in favour of reciprocity. They have charged inconsistency on the part of the Conservative party. If the Conservative party has been inconsistent, how much more so have the people of the United States been? For 45 years the United States opposed reciprocity. Why should they now endeavour to get it?
Every one knows that conditions in this country have changed. Every one knows that when we were endeavouring to get reciprocity years ago we required the market of the United States. We were a young country, undeveloped, and reciprocity in these days might have been some good to us. However, conditions are altogether changed now. It would be just as reasonable to say that because a grown-up man required a nursing bottle when he was a baby he would require it all his life. Infant Canada might have cried for the nursing bottle and the soothing syrup of reciprocity in days gone by, but to-day Canada has attained the full status of manhood, and we no longer require the reciprocity medicine. Again the charge of inconsistency does not lie at the door of the Conservative party, because the reciprocity which the Conservative party advocated in years gone by certainly had no resemblance to the Reciprocity Act as introduced by the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding).

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS - RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: What is the difference?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS - RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: The difference is that Sir John A. Macdonald, Sir John Thompson, and the other leaders of the Conservative party wanted reciprocity in its true sense. They wanted tariff for tariff and if they reduced the duty on certain articles coming into Canada they expected the United States to reduce their duties to the same level on the same goods. Would Sir John A. Macdonald or Sir John Thompson allow the products of 90,000,000 farmers in the United States to be shipped in here in competition with our farmers, when the prices are higher here than on the American side? Would they allow their products of 300,000,000 people belonging to the 12 favoured nations to be shipped in here in competition with our people?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS - RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: That is exactly what he offered in 1879.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS - RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext:
Sir John A. Macdonald would not have been guilty of such indiscretion.
I say that condtions in Canada have changed since 1879 when the National Policy was introduced and when the offer of reciprocity was made to the United States. In 1879 there was no home market in Canada. To-day 80 per cent of our products are consumed at home. Canada has developed into a great industrial country, and we are providing home markets for our farm products. In 1879 the Canadian Northwest was practically unknown, and the natural resources of the other provinces were undeveloped. We had no Canadian Pacific railway, no Canadian Northern railway and no Grand Trunk Pacific. There were no exports of any kind to Great Britain, because we did not have the shipping facilities to carry our goods, nor did we produce the goods to carry.	.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS - RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: What about 1891?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS - RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext:
To-day our shipping facilities are fully developed. Then, there is another very important point which must be borne in mind. In 1879, every Englishman in the old country was a free trader, whereas to-day even in the old country the majority of the people are in favour of tariff reform, and they believe in a measure of protection. Now that we are on the eve of forming Imperial federation-on the eve of bringing about an arrangement with Great Britain whereby our farm products will be allowed into Great Britain on a preferential basis, is it not foolhardy to enter into this agreement, which is the grave yard of Imperial federation?

In 1871 our population was 3,500,000; in 1911 it is 8,000,000. In 1868 our total trade was $129,000,000; in 1910, it amounted to $677,000,000. In 1869, our bank assets amounted to $44,000,000'; in 1911, they totalled $1,224,000,000. In 1877, our railway system covered 2,278 miles; in 1911, our railway system covers 25,000 mlies. In 1871 our manufactured products amounted to $221,000,000; in 1906, they amounted to $712,664,000. In 1871, our dairy products amounted to $1,600,000; in 1908, they amounted to $36,000,000. In 1871, we grew 16,000,000 bushels of wheat; in 1908 our wheat crop amounted to 120,000,000 bushels. In view of these facts and figures can any reasonable person say that what might have been good for Canada in the early days is good for it at the present time? ,
I want to read a most extraordinary criticism of the attitude of the Liberal party and the members of the Cabinet, taken from their own leading organ, published in the city of Ottawa. I have often wondered, when I listened to the hon. members of the government reading the old time speeches of the Conservative leaders in favour of reciprocity, if they ever noticed this editorial in the Ottawa 'Free Press'. It gives the Liberal leaders and the Liberal party a lot of wholesome advice which they should take to heart. This editorial appeared in the issue of the Ottawa 'Free Press,' of March 3rd, 1911, and is entitled 'Throw Hansard Away.' It reads as follows:
The weakest link in the argument of the Liberals in favour of reciprocity with the United States _ is the iteration and reiteration of the views and opinions of political parties and individuals in the past on that policy.
What on earth difference does it make to the people of Canada in the year of our Lord 1911 what some politicians or some party thought about the advisability of closer trade relations with the United States fifteen, twenty-five, fifty years ago?
Why bore us with long and dreary extracts from the long winded speeches of Sir Charles Tupper and his ilk in the 80's? What do we care about Lord Elgin's opinions on the policy of reciprocity years ago?
Hoes it matter a tinker's dam whether the Conservative party a quarter of a century ago favoured or didn't favour reciprocity?
Is it worth more than a trivial passing allusion that the Liberal party was at one time in favour of unrestricted reciprocity?
It does give us a pain to hear men on the Hill quoting dead speeches of the years ago, and to read in the party newspapers long extracts giving the opinions of men who, if they had not altogether passed from this sphere, are now incapacitated for public life.
In the last fifteen years a tremendous change has come over this country. We Liberals think that the splendid administration of the Laurier government was largely responsible for that change.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS - RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

WAYS AND MEANS - RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH THE UNITED STATES.

Is that good advice?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS - RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext:
Then, instead of reading speeches made at a time when conditions were entirely different from what they are to-day why does not the minister tell us what the effect of this arrangement will be upon our different industries. This agreement has never been referred to a committee composed of both political parties with power to summon witnesses and find out what the ultimate effect will be upon our industries. Instead of quoting speeches of bygone days, let the ministers busy themselves in telling us what the effect of this agreement is going to be.
They are wasting their time searching through ' Hansard ' for opinions which nobody now gives a hang about.
When they should be directing a staff of experts in the obtaining of the fullest information as to the probable effect of the agreement when it is put into operation.
That is what I urged upon the minister -a staff of experts to obtain full information of the effect of the proposed changes in the tariff. Where are your experts on

the probable effect of the agreement? Where are data and statistics to which the people are entitled? Why is this not handed over to committees as in the House of Representatives and Senate of the United States? -a committee who investigated it for two months. Why do not the ministers adopt that course and allow the interests that think they are going to be affected to appear before the committee of both Houses.
But therb has been no investigation and *there are no data, no statistics. In the case of the Grand Trunk Pacific, there was ' great haste because, as was said, Hon. George A. Cox could not wait. If this is the case it appears that the President of the United States can't wait.
Now I come to the closing part of this aiticle:
What Sir John Macdonald or Sir Charles Tupper said twenty years ago is not going to affect in the slightest the opinion of the business man of to-day who is doubtful as to the proposed policy.
Why should we be bound by the opinion expressed twenty years ago when the conditions were different from what they are to-day. Why not face this policy in the light of present conditions and judge it on its merits. And here is the completing paragraph:
Por goodness sake, let the liberal leaders chuck all the copies of ' Hansard ' away and give us something up to date.

The next question I asked the minister was this:
Were the above statements and figures present to the minds of the Canadian ministers when they executed the agreement on behalf of Canada ?
If the Minister of Finance had answered that question he would have answered, no, because no person, no representative of Canada negotiating the treaty in the interest of the farmers of this country, with those facts before him coming from the United States experts, showing that the prices of the staple products of the farm were higher in Canada than in the United States, would ever have entered into this agreement. Will the minister answer now?

The next question, No. 4, was this:
Since the date of the execution of the agreement has the government made any effort to verify the above statements and figures as set out in the United States official document No. 849?
The Minister of Finance knew well yesterday the answers to all these questions; he knew yesterday that those facts and figures of the United States authorities, which were not made public until long after the treaty was signed, were not pres-sent to his mind, and he could have answered question No. 4. He knows whether the government, in view of those facts and figures,_ showing the prices on the Canadian side higher than on the American side, had made any effort to verify them. If tlie Minister of Finance answers that question correctly, he will answer that he has made no attempt to verify those figures. But the government had determined, obstinately and pertinaciously, to stand by the two ministers, no matter what their faults of judgment may have been in making this agreement, and now they are prepared, no matter what the consequences may be to the farmers, to force this agreement upon the country. Question No. 5:
5.	Is the government aware that both the House of Representatives and the Senate of the United States referred the agreement to committees composed of both political parties before whom evidence was taken for months as to the possible effect of the agreement on the United States interests?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS - RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH THE UNITED STATES.

If the Minister of Finance answers that question he will answer it in the affirmative. He is aware that this agreement was referred to committees of both Houses of Congress, composed of both political parties, with a view of ascertaining what effect it would have upon the great interests of the United States. What information has this House in reference to this agreement? We can go out and read the newspapers, we have a little knowledge of our own; but the proper attitude for the government to take in reference to this great question was to- summon the interests that are going to be affected, and to hear them in reference to it. Were the members of any intelligent body ever before asked to commit themselves so thoroughly blindfolded to a proposal of such importance as this?
6.	Is it the intention of the government to take any evidence before any committees touching on the relative prices of farm products in the United States and Canada, or on the effect the agreement may have on Canadian interests ?
If the Minister of Finance answers that question he will answer it in this way:	It	is	not our intention to
take any evidence before committees touching the relative prices of farm products in (the two countries, because so soon as we commence to take such evidence, we will find that the prices on the Canadian side are higher than the prices on the American side., and consequently it would be detrimental to the interests of the Canadian farmers to consummate this agreement.
7.	Has the government any information now in their possession dealing with the relative prices of farm products in Canada and the United States?
I would like to ask the Minister of Finance now if they have any additional information dealing with this important matter in the nature of comparative prices. Have they sent any experts? Have they any authoritative information upon these important matters in which the farmers are so deeply interested? I will give the Minister of Finance an opportunity to answer.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS - RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext:
I want an authoritative answer from the government so that the people of Canada may have some intelligent conception of what this

agreement mean's. The fundamental position for the government to take is to find out what effect it will have. The Minister of Finance says that it is an agreement in the interests of the farmers. If it is in the interest of the farmers, surely the first step the government should have taken was to ascertain how the prices of farm products compared in the two countries.
Now, Sir, I was speaking, before I digressed, upon the charge of inconsistency that was made against the Liberal-Conservative party for having once advocated reciprocity, and now opposing it. I want to say that the reciprocity agreement that has been entered into on this occasion is not such a reciprocity agreement as was proposed by Sir John A. Macdonald; that was not the ill-advised, unfair and illogical agreement that has been negotiated^ by the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Customs. I want further to say that since 1892 the Liberal-Conservative party has not been in favour of reciprocity, and since 1898 and 1899 the Reform party, under the present leader of the government, has. been opposed to reciprocity. I want to read a few extracts showing the position the leader of the government took in days gone by. In 1899 Sir Wilfrid Laurier, speaking on this question, said:
If we know the hearts and minds of our people at present I am not making too wide a statement when I say that the general feeling in Canada is not in favour of reciprocity. There was a time when Canadians would have given many things to obtain the American market. There was a time when the market of the great cities of the union was the only market we had, but those days are past and over now. We are not depending on the American market now. It is possible they may come to us, if they do, we will teach them the lesson they have taught us.
In 1907 at the Imperial Conference the leader of the government made this statement:
There was a time when we were wanting reciprocity with the United States, but our efforts and our offers were put aside, and negatived. We have said good-bye to that trade, and we now put all our hopes upon the British trade.
Does any person now charge either the Liberal party or the Conservative party with inconsistency if they oppose reciprocity after the utterances of the leader of the government? At the Imperial Conference in 1907, the right hon. gentleman said further:
If we are to follow the lines of nature and geography between Canada, and the United States, the whole trade would flow from south to north, and from north to south. We hare 32IJ
done everything possible by canals and subsidizing railways to bring the trade from west to east and east to west so as to bring trade into British channels. All this we have done recognizing the principle of the great advantage of forcing trade within the British Empire. . . There is no boundary line except a purely conventional one over the whole territory of North America. Their habits are the same as ours, and therefore we are induced to trade and cannot help it by foroe of nature. But so far as legislation can influence trade, we have done everything possible to push our trade towards the British people as against the American people. . .
There was a time when we wanted reciprocity with the United States, but our efforts and our offers were put aside. We have said good-bye to that trade and we now put all our hopes upon the British trade.

speechtext: I would like to ask the hon. gentleman if he would read an extract or an utterance, or a resolution of any kind passed by the Conservative party, against reciprocity.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS - RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: I ask the hon. gentleman if there is any repudiation by the Conservative party, or by their responsible men, of reciprocity. I defy him to read it.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS - RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext:
If the hon. gentleman has been following the proceedings of this House he will see what the attitude of the Conservative party is upon the proposition that was made by the Minister of Finance. The Minister of Customs asks when the Conservative party was opposed to reciprocity. Why, was not the election of 1891 fought out on reciprocity? That is the kind of reciprocity that hon. gentlemen are trying to force upon the country now. Speaking about the constitutional objections, I said, Mr. Chairman, that I thought as a casual student of the principles of responsible government, that we were living in a democratic country, 'and tnat the people ruled, but we find that we are under a dictatorship headed by the right hon. leader of the government. The cabinet composed of a few members, meet in secret, they decide upon policies, they commit the country to them and then afterwards, when they have a general election, these matters are either passed over or by large campaign funds their policies are carried without a fair submission of them to the people. What do we find?-four matters of prime importance during the history of this government have been settled not by the people, but by the government themselves. The Grand Trunk proposition, by which this country was committed to an expenditure of $200,000,000, was made merely by the Liberal government, without the consent or know-

ledge of the then Minister of Railways and Canals, with Senator Cox and others. That was not submitted to the people until after it had been consummated. The honour of Canada was at stake and the country was so committed to this policy that my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) stated that if the Conservative party were elected in 1904, they would feel constrained to carry out that policy and to carry into effect the agreement with the Grand Trunk Pacific railway showing that instead of having a tentative agreement and going to the country on that, policy in a democratic way they made am agreement and crammed it down the throats of the people without a fair election. Then, in 1904 we had a general election. Was there a word then about the Autonomy Bills and the creation of the provinces in the west? Was there a statement or a whisper as to the creation of tne new provinces, as to the emasculating of these provinces and taking away from them the control of their mines, minerals, timber and educational affairs? Not a word, but during the next session they passed the Autonomy Bills that deprived these provinces of the rights of self-government that they are now claiming. Then we had the Navy Bill. We had an election in 1908, but the Navy Bill was never discussed. There was no submission to the people and no mandate from the people to enter upon an expenditure of hundreds of millions of dollars. Surely that was an extraordinary proceeding in a country where responsible government is supposed to obtain. Here we had a policy involving an enormous 'expenditure which was never discussed in any .general election although the people demanded that they should be consulted before a permanent policy was carried into effect.
Now, we have the reciprocity arrangement of 1911, making radical changes in the fiscal policy of this country, a policy that has enabled Canada to grow prosperous and develop, which policy is being changed without any consultation of tne people. Personally speaking I do not shy at the word ' blocking.' Personally speaking, I am here for the purpose of blocking reciprocity until the people have had an opportunity of being heard upon it. There is no use shying at the word. The position of the opposition was made clear by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition, in the west that, in so far as reciprocity, is concerned, reciprocity will not go upon the statute books until the people have had an opportunity to pronounce upon it.

speechtext: If time were of much moment to the government they would not remain here so long, they would dissolve and go to the country. Why keep us here in the dog days, why bring us back in July and August to discuss reciprocity when the matter should be discussed on the hustings before the people who should be permitted to pronounce upon it? One of the greatest objections to this agreement is

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS - RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext:
I am not a hanger.
Mr. SHAEPE (Ontario.) One objection to this treaty is that our natural products will become a prey to American trusts. Another is the fact that the United States with their hundred million people is an exporting country, exporting the very things that we have to sell. Another objection is that the United States and twelve other countries may compete in our market with our farmers. The fourth and strongest objection that I have discussed at some length is that the price of staple farm products are higher in Canada than in the United States. Speaking about ouif natural resources becoming a prey to the United States, everybody will admit that it is in the interests of every country to convert our raw material into the finished product within our own borders. We all approve of the pulpwood policy of the provinces of Quebec and Ontario. What does that mean? It means that these two provinces are compelling the_ people who produce pulp from Crown lands to manufacture it into paper in our own. country. That means the establishment of factories, the creation of industries, the employment of labour, and the building up of our own country. The same argument that applies to pulpwood applies also to our wheat.
We should grind our wheat into flour and save the by-products for feed. Our coarse grain should be fed to the stock and thus enrich the soil. Our stock should be converted into beef and pork ready for the market. Standing timber and saw logs should be manufactured into finished products, wood-enware, furniture, pianos, &c. The United States want raw materials, our pulp wood, our saw logs, our coarse grains wheat and stockers. _ In document No. >1418, Hon.. James Wilson, Secretary of Agriculture, in his open letter to the National Grange of February 9, 1911, says of the United States:
We get into the Canadian woods, 90,000,000 or more of ns, for timber products, things very much needed, as our home supplies are so much reduced that prices have gone up markedly in the last few years, and our own development in the future will draw heavily on what remains.
The trains that bring farm products to the United States will take farm, orchard and manufactured products back.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS - RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext:
Then farm products will go to the United States?
Mr. SHAEPE (Ontario) reading-
The _ raw material that comes from the-Canadian farm will be manufactured in the United States, and what is not needed will be sent to foreign countries.
The Canadian can furnish us with feeders,, a large per cent of the number that come to the United States are of that class.
We can handle the Canadian export grain crop with facility. If it is brought inside our borders and milled as it would be, our dairymen could use with great profit the by-products of the mills. This is the feature, bran and shorts-that makes dairy products and robs the soil.
The United States could with great profit and benefit to the land, take all the grain Canada has to sell, and devote its lands to1 less exacting crops, as is evidenced by the older prairie states farmers who grow nograin to sell, buy their flour and thereby keep up the fertility of the soil. In the western states where the farmer has turned from grain raising for sale to the production of crops to be fed to domestic animals on the farm, the new departure has been so profitable that lands in those states have risen in value to $100 to $200 per acre, and rents from $4 to $6 per acre.
Mr. Beveridge, who was here a few days ago, said in a recent speech, which will be found at page 2340 of the ' Congressional Eecord':
We have used up out natural resources so rapidly that the belated policy of conserving them has become one of our greatest national anxieties.
President Taft's message, January 26, 1911, contains this passage:
We have reached a stage in onr own development that calls for a statesmanlike and broad view of our future economic status and its requirements. We have drawn upon our natural resources in such a way as to invite attention to their necessary limit. This has properly aroused effort to conserve them, to avoid their waste, and to restrict their use to our necessities.
Ought we not then to arrange a commercial agreement with Canada, if we can, by which we shall have direct access to her great supply of natural products without an obstructing or prohibitory tariff?
The Dominion has greatly prospered. It has an active, aggressive and intelligent people. They are coming to the parting of the ways.
Would the Minister of Customs be good enough to explain what President Taft meant by that?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS - RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: My hon. friend might ask the president to explain.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS - RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext:
If that is the best answer he can give we will take it for what it is worth. The message continues:
They must soon decide whether they are to regard themselves as isolated permanently from our markets by a perpetual wall or

whether we are to be commercial friends. If we give them reason to take the former view, can we complain if they adopt methods denying access to certain of their natural resources except upon conditions quite unfavourable to us. A notable instance of such a possibility may be seen in the condition surrounding the supply of pulp wood and the manufacture of print paper for which we have made a conditional provision in the agreement, believed to be equitable. Should we not now, therefore, before their policy has become too crystallized and fixed for charge, meet them in a spirit of real concession, facilitate commerce between the two countries, and thus greatly increase the natural resources available to our people?
Free lumber we ought to have. By giving our people access to Canadian forests we shall reduce the consumption of our own, which in the hands of comparatively few owners, now have a value that requires the enlargement of our available timber resources.
That the broadening of the sources of food supplies that the opening of the timber resources of the Dominion to our needs, that the addition to the supply of raw materials will be limited to no particulaar section does not require demonstration.
Are these messages not pregnant with warnings to us who pride ourselves on being Canadians? What is the burden of their song? To what do they attach importance? Baw materials ! Every page bristling with the words raw materials. Raw mater ials ! Raw materials ! They want us to cut down our timber our grain crops, our pulp wood, harvest our raw materials-ship them
Showing that the United States is pursuing a policy of encouraging the working up of the raw materials into the finished product in their own country. The policy of this administration is to encourage the export of raw materials-to let the United States get the possession of our raw materials on which they can employ their own labour and capital, and send back the fin-Mr. SHARPE (Ontario).
in that condition to the United States, let them with their labour and capital work them up to manufactured goods and sell them back to us!
Are we to be a party to such a policy? Are we to be a party to such self-suppression? Are we to be the hewers of wood and the drawers of water to the United States people?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS - RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: Is there anything that gives the Americans access to our raw materials that they have not now?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS - RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext:
I say the minister by this agreement is facilitating the export of raw materials to the United States, and by thus encouraging that export and by allowing the clause regarding pulp wood to be inserted in the agreement, is trying to facilitate the export of pulp-wood in the raw condition, and thus to put the screws on the provinces to change their laws in regard to the export of pulpwood.
I wish now to submit some figures that show that the United States are shipping less raw material, and more finished products from their country.
